articles.title: Hotels need minimum standards to keep women safe, committee told
articles.summary: MPs hear calls for national hotel safety standards after an outcry over a sexual assault at a Travelodge.
articles.body:
Hotels should face national minimum standards to protect female guests, witnesses have told a parliamentary committee examining safety in the industry.

The hearing followed an independent review into security failings at Travelodge after a woman was sexually assaulted at one of its hotels in Maidenhead, Berkshire.

The review's author, Paul Greaney KC, said room intrusions had become so common they were treated as something to be tolerated, while Travelodge's interim chief executive admitted the company had not taken guest safety seriously enough.

Committee chair and Labour MP Olivia Bailey said the evidence showed not enough was being done to protect women and called for "concrete action".

The one-off parliamentary session heard evidence from hotel chains including Travelodge, Premier Inn UK and Z Hotels, alongside women's safety organisations.

Three women giving evidence revealed they had previously barricaded their hotel room doors to feel safer during their stays.

UK Hospitality chief executive Allen Simpson also recalled inadvertently revealing the location of a domestic violence victim to their abuser while working as a hotel receptionist earlier in his career.

Greaney's independent review, commissioned by Travelodge, found the company had failed the Maidenhead victim "at every stage" .

The woman had spoken to the BBC after her attacker gained access to her room by lying to reception staff.

Other guests subsequently came forward with similar experiences of security problems at Travelodge and other hotel chains.

In August, Travelodge's chief executive Jo Boydell stepped down ahead of the publication of the independent review.

Greaney told the committee: "All hotels need to have a policy designed to ensure room security and to implement it by training their staff."

Emma Lingley-Clark, chief executive of the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, argued that guest safety should be treated like other basic standards expected of hotels.

She said: "This should be considered in exactly the same light."

Travelodge's interim chief executive Ray Reidy apologised again to the Maidenhead victim and others affected by the company's failings.

He added: "Historically, speaking for Travelodge, I don't think we have taken it seriously. I don't think we did that intentionally. I don't think we'd deliberately ignored it. But I don't think we had given it, as highlighted in the report, the focus that it needed."

"I would like to think that this is a milestone instance in the sector.

"We are still not where we want to be, but we are taking it incredibly seriously in terms of how we move forward."

Speaking after the hearing, chair Olivia Bailey, who is also MP for Reading West and Mid Berkshire, said: "There have been lots of examples that we've seen in the media that people have told the committee of women's safety just not being taken seriously enough in hotels."

"It is clear from the evidence we've heard today that not enough is being done.

"There needs to be a wholesale culture change.

"We need to make sure we don't just get warm words here. We need to make sure we have concrete action.

"What we'll be doing as a committee is considering what that concrete action might need to look like".

Kyran Smith was jailed in February for seven-and-a-half years following the Travelodge assault in December 2022.

articles.title: Cabinet ministers advised to avoid foreign travel; Parliament session likely by December 15
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Amid continuing suspense over the government’s plan to push the delimitation bill, Cabinet ministers have been asked to avoid planning overseas
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Amid continuing suspense over the government’s plan to push the delimitation bill, Cabinet ministers have been asked to avoid planning overseas travel and engagements and remain prepared for Parliament to be convened at short notice, possibly anytime before mid-December.PM Narendra Modi is learnt to have hinted at the likelihood of a parliamentary session by December 15 at the Cabinet meeting chaired by him Wednesday. Government sources have maintained that the Constitution amendment bill to implement the women’s reservation law from the 2029 general elections and increase the strength of Lok Sabha by around 50 per cent is likely to be introduced in the next sitting of Parliament.The government’s decision not to prorogue the monsoon session, which was adjourned sine die on Aug 13, has also fuelled speculation that it’s meant to facilitate early resumption of Parliamentary proceedings. Keeping the session alive allows the parliamentary affairs ministry to reconvene both Houses at three days’ notice without going through the process of summoning a fresh session.Although NDA has maintained a tight lid on its legislative strategy, senior functionaries have expressed confidence that the government will secure the two-thirds majority required to pass the Constitution amendment bill. This is a significant challenge, given that the opposition’s united stand had thwarted the government’s attempt to get the legislation through when it was first introduced in April.The political landscape, however, has changed since then, with the INDIA bloc showing signs of fragmentation. The government is understood to be factoring in these developments while assessing its numbers and prospects of securing the required support.The proposed legislation seeks to link the implementation of women’s reservation with a delimitation exercise that would redraw parliamentary constituencies and substantially expand Lok Sabha’s strength. The proposed expansion and the methodology for delimitation have been among the principal points of contention, with opposition parties raising concerns over their potential implications for the political representation of states. However, the government has tried to assuage concerns by saying that each state‘s share of seats in the Lok Sabha will increase by 50 per cent.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
articles.summary: The musician, who co-wrote some of the band's biggest hits, had been treated for prostate cancer.
articles.body:
Andy Taylor, the guitarist for the pop group Duran Duran, has died at the age of 65.

Born in Tynemouth, he co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits, including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film; and also worked with artists like Robert Palmer, Rod Stewart and Belinda Carlisle.

In a statement, his bandmates said Taylor had fought "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer" and "passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23 November".

His wife, Tracey, said the musician "was the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day".

Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off

The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.

He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.

The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.

Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.

"Andy was there at the very beginning of our story," said his bandmates Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor (his bandmates were unrelated, despite sharing the same last name).

"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.

"Our thoughts are with his wife Tracey, his children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and grandson Albie. They all loved him deeply and we ask that their privacy be respected at this very difficult time."

Duran Duran were one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, and its five members became global hearththrobs.

Their indelible hooks and airbrushed music videos found a natural home on the newly launched MTV, giving their career a huge boost in the US.

They became so popular in the States that the press labeled them the leaders of a "Second British Invasion" of the charts - alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Human League and Eurythmics.

During a hiatus in 1984, Andy and John Taylor enlisted Robert Palmer for their successful but short-lived side project the Power Station.

The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran, after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid.

"We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy.

"We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral."

He went on to play on Robert Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.

After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.

In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion.

When the group took the stage, singer Simon Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.

Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.

"Andy never took the easy musical route," said Le Bon in a personal statement marking his friend's death.

"His overdrive, overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later.

"There's a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart. It'll never close up; I won't let it. I will miss him & love him for all my days."

Taylor is survived by his wife, Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982.

"For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first," she wrote in her statement.

"Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home."

She continued: "Andy faced the last few years with so much courage and determination. He never gave up, fighting until the very end, never losing his love of life.

"The kindness and support shown to him by fans from all over the world throughout his illness brought him immense comfort and strength, and for that we will always be grateful."

articles.title: What Happened to Alice Huang, the Woman at the Center of Nvidia’s Scandal?
articles.summary: U.S. intelligence found no evidence that Beijing directed Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia’s CEO, but the former Megaspeed executive still faces entry bans and s...
articles.body:
While Jensen Huang has returned to the helm of Nvidia following a brief but dramatic departure, the Chinese businesswoman at the center of the scandal that threatened his career remains largely out of public view.

U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staffers on Tuesday that they had found no evidence that Alice Huang was instructed by Chinese intelligence to spy on the Nvidia chief executive, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the classified briefing.

Although officials claimed that she had contacted China's intelligence service during the affair, they found no indication that she had passed on significant intelligence. The assessment could change if new evidence emerges.

The findings mark a significant development in a controversy that has shaken Silicon Valley—and the whole global economy alongside it—and heightened tensions over China's access to advanced American technology.

But for Alice Huang, questions surrounding her business activities, legal situation and future remain unresolved.

From business executive to national security controversy

Also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le, Alice Huang is a Hong Kong resident who previously led Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing company that became a major customer of Nvidia.

The company originated as the overseas subsidiary of a Chinese video game business before shifting into artificial intelligence infrastructure. It became an official Nvidia cloud partner in November 2023.

According to corporate records cited by the Associated Press, Huang ceased to be a registered director of Megaspeed in November 2023, although Singaporean authorities identified her as its chief executive, chairperson and a key controller when they investigated the company in 2025.

Megaspeed said on November 15 that Huang had formally departed on August 30, 2025, and no longer held any position within the company. It declined to discuss her private affairs and maintained that its business operations were lawful.

Huang's troubles with Singaporean authorities began well before the allegations of espionage became public.

Singapore launched an investigation in February 2025 into suspected false declarations involving purchases of computer servers and their eventual destinations.

Police questioned Huang in June that year and retained her passport to ensure her availability during the investigation.

In February 2026, authorities determined that there was insufficient evidence to establish that she had committed offences related to the suspected false declarations.

However, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said investigators believed Huang had knowingly supplied inaccurate information to minimize her involvement in Megaspeed.

She received a formal warning and was prohibited from returning to Singapore. Authorities returned her passport on February 26, and she left the country that day.

Taiwanese authorities have also revoked her entry permit.

Speaking in Australia on Tuesday, Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong reiterated that authorities had found no grounds to pursue prosecution against Huang, although investigations into Megaspeed were continuing.

Singapore has explicitly stated that its investigation of Huang did not concern espionage.

Bloomberg reported on November 12, citing anonymous sources, that Huang was in Beijing and that Chinese security officials were aware of her presence there. Her current whereabouts have not been independently confirmed.

Beijing has rejected the espionage allegations, while Huang herself has remained publicly silent in recent reporting.

Meanwhile, scrutiny of her business network continues to intensify.

On Wednesday, Reuters reported that companies connected to Huang's relatives and business associates had secured financing against AI servers and computing modules valued at $270 million in China.

The financial records did not establish whether the equipment contained chips subject to US export restrictions. Huang could not be reached for comment by Reuters .

The revelations followed Washington's decision on Monday to add Megaspeed and several related businesses to its trade blacklist.

While the latest intelligence assessment weakens the allegation that Huang was engaged in a Beijing-directed espionage operation, it does not settle the separate questions surrounding her commercial connections.

For now, Jensen Huang has reclaimed his position at one of the world's most influential technology companies. Alice Huang's professional future, however, remains uncertain.

articles.title: 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed: What to know
articles.summary: For the first time in its history, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been rescheduled due to weather, shifting to Saturday amid a forecast of high winds.
articles.body: The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed ahead of an expected nor'easter in New York City, marking the first time the parade has been rescheduled due to weather. The parade has been moved from Thursday to Saturday due to a forecast of strong winds and heavy rain, according to The Associated Press. All the balloons that were filled up on Wednesday will be deflated and returned to New Jersey for storage until Saturday. "With severe weather expected on Thanksgiving Day and in close partnership with our city partners, the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will now march on Saturday, November 28th," Macy's Thanksgiving Parade Executive Producer Will Coss told reporters. WORST AIRPORTS FOR THANKSGIVING TRAVEL CHAOS RANKED AS MAJOR US HUBS TOP LIST Coss noted that organizers have spent two years preparing for Saturday's event. "Our team is now working through the complex operational logistics required to bring the Parade to life on Saturday, and we will share additional details as they are finalized," Macy's said in a statement. "We are incredibly grateful to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who make this extraordinary tradition possible. We can’t wait to celebrate 100 years of Parade magic together on Saturday." Spectators typically watch workers fill up the balloons the night before the parade, but there won't be an "inflation night" on Friday, he said. "It's the only inflation we support here in New York City," Mayor Zohran Mamdani joked. Macy's was working with school bands from outside the city who were in town so they could perform in Saturday's parade, Coss said. "It will be spectacular. I promise you. It will be the parade that we set out to deliver, so I look forward to sharing it with everyone," he said. A Thanksgiving storm is expected to hit New York City and the tri-state area with heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding in some places expected. An area of low pressure developing off the Southeast coast will push northward into the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast beginning Wednesday night. The storm is expected to intensify through Thanksgiving Day before clearing out on Friday, according to the FOX Forecast Center and the National Weather Service. The iconic parade draws thousands of spectators along the 2½-mile route, which begins in Manhattan's Upper West Side to Herald Square on 34th Street, the site of the Macy's department store. Mamdani said the parade is part of the city's iconic culture, but that public safety could not be compromised. "I know that many New Yorkers, myself included, as well as millions around the world, were looking forward to the parade being held tomorrow," he said. "Generation after generation has watched SpongeBob and Spider-Man soar down our streets, and has taken in Garfield floating down Sixth Avenue. And I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences." "Yet safety has to come first," he added. articles.title: A Colorado ranching family's use of a three-mile road across neighbouring land dates back to 1958, but new owners challenged their access; a November 12 ruling upheld a permanent injunction
articles.summary: A road used by a ranching family for decades can become the subject of a property dispute when ownership changes and questions arise over who has the
articles.body: A road used by a ranching family for decades can become the subject of a property dispute when ownership changes and questions arise over who has the right to cross the land. In Colorado, a family that had used a three-mile road to move livestock and equipment since 1958 lost its claim to a permanent access right after the new owners of the neighbouring ranch challenged its continued use. The Colorado Court of Appeals upheld a permanent injunction against the family on November 12, 2026, finding that the road had been used with the previous owner's permission during at least part of the 18-year statutory period.According to the court's memorandum opinion in Camilletti Ranch Properties, LLC v. Seely, available on Justia, the dispute concerned a road crossing nearly 2,000 acres of ranchland in Routt County. The appellate court affirmed the district court's decision that the Seely family had not established a prescriptive easement, which would have given them a legally recognised right to continue using the road without needing the landowner's permission.How the ranching family's road access beganThe history of the dispute goes back to 1958, when Lowry Seely, the father of David Seely and grandfather of Sue Voloshin, purchased a ranch in Routt County. In 1971, David acquired a neighbouring property and also used it for ranching operations. The adjoining land was owned by Harvey and Velda Wyman, and later by the Velda L Wyman Revocable Trust. Their property covered almost 2,000 acres and contained an unpaved road approximately three miles long, running from northwest to southeast.From at least 1958 through 1976, the Seely family and its predecessors used the road twice a year to transport livestock and equipment between their properties and US Forest Service grazing parcels. The family continued using it after the property changed hands. Darrell and Carol Camilletti purchased the Wyman property in 2021 and transferred it to Camilletti Ranch Properties LLC (CRP) in 2024. The Seely family continued crossing the land twice annually, but the new ownership eventually led to disagreement over whether the family had an independent legal right to use the road.Why the new owners challenged the accessIn 2023, CRP learned that the Seelys claimed a prescriptive easement over the road and intended to use it without requesting permission. The company filed a lawsuit seeking an injunction, a declaration of its property rights and damages for trespass and conversion. The Seelys filed a counterclaim arguing that their long-standing use had established a prescriptive easement.Under Colorado law, a prescriptive easement is a non-exclusive right to use another person's land for a particular purpose. To establish one, the claimant generally must demonstrate that the use was open or notorious and continuous for at least 18 years. Once these requirements are established, the law presumes that the use was adverse. However, the property owner can rebut that presumption by demonstrating that the use was permitted.The district court ruled in favour of CRP following a bench trial. It granted a permanent injunction, rejected the family's easement claims and awarded nominal damages for trespass.Why the appeals court upheld the injunctionThe central question was whether the Wymans had allowed the Seely family to use the road with their permission. There was no direct evidence of an express agreement between Lowry Seely and Harvey Wyman. However, the district court considered the surrounding circumstances, including Wyman's reputation for closely monitoring his property and the presence of gates at both entrances to the road by 1964.Although there was no evidence that the gates had been locked during the relevant 1958-1976 period, Wyman eventually locked them in 1988 following a disagreement involving a hunter and commercial hunting activities. The district court inferred that Wyman had installed the gates to maintain control over his property and that the family had used the road with his implied permission.The Seelys challenged this conclusion, arguing that the court had relied on speculation rather than evidence. They also contended that implied permission required proof of the landowner's words or actions. The appeals court disagreed. It explained that permission could be inferred from surrounding circumstances and did not always require an explicit conversation or agreement. It found sufficient evidence to support the conclusion that Wyman had permitted the family's use during at least part of the statutory period.The court acknowledged that the case was a close one and that some of the district court's reasoning was inconsistent. Nevertheless, it concluded that the evidence supported the finding of permissive use. Because use that begins with permission cannot develop into a prescriptive easement, the family's claim failed. The court also rejected David Seely's separate arguments that he could combine earlier family use with his own or establish an independent easement through his personal use of the road. The November 12, 2026, ruling affirmed the district court's judgment and left the permanent injunction and nominal trespass damages in place. The opinion was issued as an unpublished decision under Colorado Appellate Rule 35(e).You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt settle legal battle over French winery
articles.summary: The Hollywood A-listers' legal battle focused on the vineyard they bought in 2008 and where they wed six years later.
articles.body:
Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle over her sale of a stake in their French vineyard, which unfolded amid a bitter divorce.

"We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further," said the Hollywood stars' representatives in a joint statement.

They bought a controlling interest in Château Miraval in 2008 and wed there six years later.

In the lawsuit, Pitt , 62 , argued that Jolie, 51, acted without his permission in selling her share in the winery to a Russian oligarch. She counter-sued, accusing Pitt of drunkenly attacking her and their children on a flight, prompting her to file for divorce in 2016.

The settlement announced on Wednesday resolves both of their respective legal actions.

"Any comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us," said the statement from their representatives.

Pitt's lawsuit had accused Jolie of seeking "to inflict harm" on him when she sold her stake in their co-owned vineyard, which he claimed had forced him to partner with "a stranger with poisonous associations and intentions".

The Fight Club star said he and Jolie had agreed not to sell their stakes in the venue without the permission of the other.

It was alleged that Jolie had sold her share to a Luxembourg-based spirits manufacturer controlled by Russian oligarch Yuri Shefler, without Pitt's knowledge.

Jolie hit back with her own lawsuit, accusing Pitt of grabbing her by the head and attacking two of their children during a 2016 private jet flight trip.

Pitt also verbally abused and poured alcohol on his family during the flight from France to Los Angeles, her lawsuit had alleged.

Her lawyers alleged Pitt began shouting, accusing her of being "too deferential" to their six children - aged eight to 15 at the time.

Pitt was not charged following a police investigation into the incident and he denied the allegations.

They reached a divorce settlement late last year after an eight-year legal battle.

It is understood that Pitt's litigation with Stoli Group, a beverage company owned by the Russian oligarch, is ongoing.

At the time of their 2014 marriage, Pitt and Jolie were among the most lucrative names in Hollywood.

They met on the set of the 2005 film Mr and Mrs Smith and were soon dubbed Brangelina by the press.

The marriage was Pitt's second after a relationship with Friends star Jennifer Aniston.

It was Jolie's third, after actors Billy Bob Thornton and Jonny Lee Miller.

Jolie adopted her first child, Maddox, from Cambodia in 2002 a few months after he was born. Pitt later adopted him after he and Jolie had begun their relationship.

In 2005, the pair adopted daughter Zahara from Ethiopia when she was a few months old.

The couple's first biological child, Shiloh, was born in Namibia in 2006.

Their son Pax was adopted at the age of three from Vietnam in 2007, and twins Knox and Vivienne were born in 2008.

Since the couple split, four of the six children have legally changed their last name to Jolie rather than Jolie-Pitt, according to court filings citied by Hollywood press.

articles.title: Long waits 'a tragedy' as thousands seek ADHD and autism assessments
articles.summary: A GP warns that long waits for ADHD and autism assessments mean those most in need are not being seen.
articles.body:
A GP has warned that long waits for ADHD and autism assessments are creating a situation where the people most in need are not being seen.

According to experts, demand has risen so sharply in recent years that it now far exceeds what the mental health system can cope with.

New figures seen by BBC Scotland News suggest more than 38,000 adults are waiting for neurodevelopmental assessments, with at least 14,000 of them waiting longer than two years.

Dr Marianne McCallum, who represents the Deep End group of doctors working in Scotland's most deprived areas, said it was a "tragedy" that people who really needed a diagnosis because they were not coping could not be seen by a specialist.

She said those who had the most to gain from a diagnosis were currently the least likely to get it, with a huge rise in private referrals creating a two-tier system.

Dr McCallum, who works in the Ferguslie Park area of Paisley, said: "It's just become a bit of a mess, because there's a bottleneck and the secondary services are overwhelmed.

"In primary care we're trying to hold a lot of this without any extra resource."

Dr McCallum said some patients were influenced by social media.

"I've had people who've come in saying they think they need an ADHD assessment and actually when I've spoken to them, the problem is dyslexia," she said.

She said this meant some people who had a really significant lifelong neurodevelopmental condition were unable to access services.

"It is a tragic situation, particularly for people who really could do with the diagnosis," Dr McCallum said.

"Sometimes they lose their job because they're not coping and they snap and that's it. So I think it is a tragedy."

Autism is a lifelong developmental condition that affects the way a person communicates, interacts, and processes information.

There is no medical treatment for the condition.

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) can affect different brain functions including communication, emotions and attention.

Drugs that can help symptoms can only be prescribed by the NHS if the patient has an NHS diagnosis, or under what is called a "shared care" agreement.

But most GPs will not offer this for a private diagnosis.

Lynne Balmain is waiting for an NHS assessment after paying £1,000 for a private ADHD diagnosis from a clinic in Glasgow last year.

The 54-year-old said: "I wasn't sleeping at night, I was aware of the speed that my brain was functioning at, it was constant.

"I was catastrophising over simple day-to-day things that everybody does."

Lynne said she was currently paying for medication with no indication of when she will be seen by the NHS.

"I can't really afford to keep this going but from a mental health and well-being perspective, I can't afford not to be medicated either so I'm being forced to choose," she said.

In recent years, Scotland has seen an unprecedented rise in the number of people seeking assessment and support for both ADHD and autism.

But a 2025 report by the Royal College of Psychiatrists in Scotland (RCPsychiS) said there was no national approach to meeting that demand.

It found the scale of need "far exceeded" what Scotland's mental health system could deliver.

The report found people with autism and ADHD were at higher risk of developing other mental health conditions and at a higher risk of suicide, which could be reduced with timely diagnosis and care.

It also said those with more severe mental illness faced longer delays accessing urgent care.

The data tracking website ADHD.Scot asked all of Scotland's 14 regional health boards how many people were waiting for an assessment, how long they were waiting, and how many assessments had been carried out in the past year.

Nine responded with full figures but five health boards could not provide comparable data.

Overall, the figures suggested that only 1,575 assessments were carried out on the NHS for neurodevelopmental conditions in the last year for which data was available.

NHS Lothian, which had the most people waiting (13,253), only saw 537 patients for their first appointment last year.

In Greater Glasgow and Clyde, more than 9,000 adults were waiting for an ADHD assessment, with about 559 seen in the year to March 2026.

For autism, Highland had 372 adults on the list for assessments, of which 290 had been waiting over two years and the longest wait was about seven years.

Only eight people in Highland received a first appointment with a specialist in the last year.

Last week, the Court of Session ruled against a man who had taken NHS Tayside to court, claiming it was impossible for him to get an ADHD assessment after being referred by his GP.

His case was that the health board's policy now excluded those who did not also have other mental health conditions.

The judge accepted the health board's position that there had been no change in policy and, in fact, it was the huge increase in demand for assessments that meant his case had not been a priority for those managing local waiting lists.

The Scottish government is expected to publish plans to improve neurodevelopmental support for adults in the coming weeks.

A spokesperson said: "Demand for adult neurodevelopmental diagnosis and support has risen significantly in recent years, placing considerable pressure on services across Scotland.

"We recognise that this can be a frustrating and uncertain time for people. However, support should be available based on people's individual needs, rather than having to wait for a diagnosis for help."

articles.title: Aboriginal artefacts returned by University of Aberdeen
articles.summary: Traditional shields, digging sticks and sacred men's objects have been returned to the Karajarri people.
articles.body:
Aboriginal artefacts collected almost 100 years ago in Australia have been returned by the University of Aberdeen.

Anthropologist Dr Ralph Piddington collected the objects in 1930 and 1931 when he was researching in Western Australia while studying at the University of Sydney.

The traditional shields, digging sticks and sacred men's objects were later brought to Scotland, but have now been returned to the Karajarri people.

The university said there was no evidence to suggest the items had been obtained unethically, but their return reflected a "shared understanding" they should be held by the Karajarri community.

The artefacts are said to form a key part of their culture.

More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland

Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds

The university has carried out repatriations before.

The institution made the latest repatriation announcement at a ceremony with Karajarri representatives and Australian government officials.

It was the culmination of three years of work involving the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies (AIATSIS) cultural heritage program, Karajarri elders, and the university.

Martin Bin Rashid, the chief executive officer of the Karajarri Traditional Lands Association, said he wanted to acknowledge the "significance" of the repatriation.

"We welcome home an important collection of our cultural heritage that has been away from our country and our people for almost 100 years," he explained.

"These objects are much more than museum items. They are part of who we are and carry the history, identity, knowledge and cultural connections of our ancestors.

"Our culture is living and our cultural heritage belongs with our people."

Neil Curtis, the head of collections at the of the University of Aberdeen, said: "This ceremony is not simply about the return of objects.

"It is about how addressing the legacies of museum collections can increase cultural understanding and support people and communities to revitalise cultural knowledge and practice."

Curtis described it as an "honour" to return the items to the community from which they originated.

"They will continue to hold cultural significance and provide an important connection to Karajarri heritage," he said.

articles.title: A Minnesota couple put two waterfront lots up for sale, but their neighbour posted a sign denying harbour access and moored his boat in front; a November 23 appeals ruling upheld $64,061 in legal fees
articles.summary: A Minnesota couple's attempt to sell two waterfront properties was disrupted after their neighbour challenged their right to access the adjoining harbour,
articles.body: A Minnesota couple's attempt to sell two waterfront properties was disrupted after their neighbour challenged their right to access the adjoining harbour, put up a sign making the claim and parked his boat along their shoreline. The dispute went to court, with the Minnesota Court of Appeals ruling on Monday, that the neighbour had wrongly interfered with the couple's property rights.According to the ruling, the court upheld an earlier decision in favour of Brandon and Sara Buckingham. It also confirmed that they were entitled to $64,061 in legal fees, rejecting their neighbour Francis Branch's challenge to the award.The disagreement began after the Buckinghams listed their two properties for sale in 2024. The plots are part of the Port Mille Lacs South Harbor development and are located beside a stretch of water connected to Lake Mille Lacs. Branch owns the neighbouring property.The couple initially received calls from people interested in buying the plots. However, the interest stopped after Branch placed a sign near their property declaring it private and stating "No Harbor Access". He also moored his boat in the water directly alongside their shoreline.The Buckinghams said the sign and the boat affected both their access to the harbour and their efforts to sell the properties. They asked Branch through their lawyer to remove the sign, warning that they would take legal action if he continued to dispute their rights. Branch refused, maintaining that the couple had no right to access the harbour.Property documents support couple's claimThe Buckinghams took the matter to court in December 2024, accusing Branch of making false claims about their property rights and interfering with their use of the land. They also raised a trespass claim.The district court ruled in the couple's favour on two claims, finding that Branch had wrongly challenged their ownership rights and interfered with their enjoyment of the properties. The couple later withdrew the trespass claim and sought compensation for their legal expenses.Branch challenged the findings, arguing that the couple did not have the right to access South Harbor. However, the appeals court found that their property documents clearly supported their claim.The title certificates for both Buckingham properties included rights allowing the owners to reach the water's edge and keep boats in the harbour. The same provision was also present in the documents held by previous owners.Branch owned a one-fourth share of a portion of the submerged land beneath the harbour. But the court said this ownership did not cancel the access rights recorded in the Buckinghams' property documents.The court also rejected Branch's reliance on an earlier ruling involving the same harbour. That case concerned whether property owners could remove existing docks, not whether they could reach the water from their land. The judges said it did not support his claim that the Buckinghams had no harbour access.Earlier dispute also raised questions The court also considered Branch's involvement in an earlier disagreement over the boundaries of properties around South Harbor.In that dispute, a proposed change to the boundaries would have created a strip of land between several waterfront properties and the water. This could have prevented the owners from reaching the harbour without crossing land belonging to others.Branch had acquired an ownership interest in this strip of land. He had also supported an earlier legal action against other property owners over access to the harbour.However, the case was dismissed after the proposed boundary changes were found not to have been properly approved or communicated to the affected owners.The appeals court said Branch's knowledge of these earlier proceedings was important. It found that he had reason to know that his ownership interest did not take away the Buckingham properties' existing access rights.The judges also considered the original developer's permits for the harbour. These required the extended water area to remain open and unobstructed for public use. State authorities had also stated that the harbour was an extension of public waters, although people still needed to obtain legal access to reach it.Taking these circumstances together, the court rejected Branch's argument that he had made the claims in good faith. It upheld the finding that he had acted with disregard for the truth when he challenged the couple's access rights.Court says boat interfered with property use and saleThe appeals court separately examined the boat parked along the Buckinghams' shoreline. Branch did not dispute that he had moored his old deck boat in the water beside their properties.Evidence before the court showed that the boat blocked the shoreline, making it difficult for the couple to access South Harbor. The judges also found that the boat, along with the sign, had affected their attempts to sell the land.The couple had received enquiries from potential buyers before the sign appeared. Those calls stopped afterwards, and they were unable to sell the properties.The court agreed that Branch's actions had interfered with the couple's use and enjoyment of their land. It therefore upheld the lower court's decision on this issue as well.Branch also challenged the $64,061 legal fee award. He argued that the couple should receive fees only for work directly connected to their successful claim over the false property statements.The appeals court disagreed. It said the three claims arose from the same events and involved overlapping work. The fact that the couple did not pursue the trespass claim to a final decision did not mean their legal expenses had to be reduced.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Wang Fuk Court: A renovation was meant to improve these Hong Kong homes - it ended in a blaze that killed 168
articles.summary: A year after one of Hong Kong's deadliest fires, families left behind are still waiting for justice.
articles.body:
It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.

At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it.

It was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user - was trapped inside their home.

"I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC.

When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police.

She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said.

Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second - an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found.

It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, said the report.

"It was ferocious… I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau.

She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer.

The body of Lau Man Kwong was eventually found by rescuers - he had locked himself inside the toilet.

"He was wearing his slippers, sitting on the toilet and clutching his identity card," said his wife, who added that she escaped death "by the narrowest margin".

"I would have held onto my husband and died with him.

"He was such a good person. I just don't understand why he had to die in such a terrible way."

Mr Lau and his wife moved into Wang Fuk Court in 1983 - the year the building was completed.

She recalls an idyllic life - a family with three children who were able to grow up close to the sea and spend weekends playing at a nearby park.

"All three of my children adored my husband… He could be very stern, and I was the only woman who could make him laugh."

In 2024, mandated renovations began in Wang Fuk Court.

In Hong Kong, all buildings over 30 years old have to undergo an inspection - and any necessary renovations as a result.

Like many building complexes in Hong Kong, Wang Fuk Court had a management committee that oversaw things like building repairs. As many as 57 construction companies submitted bids. But the company that won, Prestige Construction and Engineering (PC&E), submitted the most expensive bid at HK$336m ($42.8m; £32.4m).

Residents, many of whom were over 65, had to bear the cost. The hefty bills triggered protests but eventually, the contract was signed. But once the renovations began in July 2024, residents were unhappy.

Among the complaints was that workers constantly smoked on site, dropping cigarette butts everywhere.

The 1,154 page report suggested the fire was caused by a lit cigarette.

There were also complaints about most of Wang Fuk Court's eight buildings having their windows taped over with foam boards to stop debris falling in - blocking daylight or any sort of view at all, for months.

All eight buildings were also covered in a protective mesh netting and bamboo scaffolding.

The report also found that after typhoons damaged the original scaffolding nets in 2025, cheaper non-fire-retardant replacements were chosen - something that was done as a "cost-saving measure at the expense of the safety of the residents".

Residents had filed nearly 140 complaints to six government departments, including the fire services and the buildings departments, in and after 2024, but these were largely ignored, the report went on to say.

It also revealed that a staff member of the estate's property manager, ISS, had turned off the power supply to the fire alarms in all eight buildings - which is why no alarms rang on the day itself.

ISS later told the BBC it had "reviewed and reinforced its procedures [and] staff training" in Hong Kong, adding that it takes the findings of the report "very seriously".

But for those who did manage to flee their homes - the emergency staircase turned out to be another death trap. Windows were removed from some fire escape stairwells to create temporary openings for workers - letting in smoke and cutting off vital escape routes.

Dozens, including Christy's husband, died in such stairwells.

Christy, who wanted to be identified only by her first name, says her husband was at home alone when the fire broke out. She only found out about it when her friends sent her messages about it. By the time she made it to the apartment complex, it was already cordoned off.

She found out later that he had died of smoke inhalation in the stairwell, something she says that is at least of some consolation to her.

"My husband's body would have been burnt and he would have been in more pain if he was at home. At the very least… his suffering was minimal."

Christy says her family had just celebrated their eldest child's ninth birthday the day before - they had saved some leftover cake in the fridge to eat the next day. Their father never got to eat it.

Both children have been deeply affected by the loss of their father.

Her youngest child, a seven-year-old boy, had "covered his ears and yelled" when he was first told what had happened to his father.

He now often comforts his mother, saying he will take care of her as he is the only man in the family.

"He hides his emotions. A seven-year-old child should not behave this way, and I feel heartbroken," says Christy, who has herself been diagnosed with PTSD and depression.

Her daughter has "extreme thoughts" she says, and channels her emotions through art.

She turned 10 on Wednesday, but this year, there was no birthday celebration in sight.

Her birthday, she says, will now instead be a day to commemorate her father.

Wang Fuk Court's problems date back to before the renovations began.

The management company hired to oversee and supervise the project, Will Power, conspired with PC&E to defraud residents in Wang Fuk Court, according to the city's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).

Although PC&E was found to have breached safety requirements and violated building department rules for multiple previous projects, homeowners at Wang Fuk Court were told that they had a clean record.

The ICAC alleges that this was part of a lucrative scheme, with Will Power's director Wong Hap-yin, along with other individuals, laundering over $5m in suspected proceeds from the tendering process from Wang Fuk Court, among other housing projects.

Once PC&E cinched the contract, Will Power's registered inspector - an individual meant to oversee the renovations - merely rubber-stamped the documents, without having actually conducted any inspections personally, the report added.

Will Power has been since liquidated and PC&E could not be reached for a response.

Both companies - Will Power and PC&E - and seven individuals have been charged with 25 counts of offences including including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion.

Four of them are still in custody but none of the cases have gone to trial yet.

The report said both companies involved were the "main culprits responsible".

But it also directed heavy criticism at authorities, saying that "no government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum".

One expert, Prof John Burns of Hong Kong University, had called the event the "largest governance crisis" that authorities have faced since 2020 - a reference to the controversial National Security Law that was passed in that year.

On the day the report was released, almost one year after the fire, Hong Kong's housing chief Winnie Ho resigned and the city's top leader John Lee apologised for the first time, promising that a "large number" of reforms would be rolled out.

Five months after the fire, Mrs Lau was allowed into her flat for the first time to collect any personal belongings that might have remained.

In her first visit, she was given just three hours to retrieve 40 years' worth of belongings.

Pictures taken from the visit show a home that has been utterly burned out - with every surface blackened and soot covering the floor.

"I almost fainted when I saw what had become of my home. I don't understand how the home I had built, such a warm and beautiful home, could end up like this," said Mrs Lau.

Her children, who came with her, described the house as a "war zone". Among the rubble, they found broken pieces of a piggy bank that Mr Lau had dutifully filled with coins every day for the past 20 years.

"Everyone in our family knew it was his favourite possession. The piggy bank died with him," said Mrs Lau.

Mrs Lau and her daughter have since rented a place nearby to live - and she is worried about how she is going to afford a new house.

The government has said it will spend $867m (£663m) to acquire affected flats - but Mrs Lau says it is not nearly enough to buy a similarly sized flat in the area.

Still, her family was in a better position than many others, she said.

"I lost my husband but many families lost multiple family members... Babies less than a year old died. "

Stories have emerged of some of the other victims - a six-month-old who died alongside her 68-year-old grandmother when the fire broke out.

The bodies of an Indonesian domestic helper and the elderly person she worked for were found huddled together.

As for Christy, she says she is planning to file a lawsuit against those responsible for the fire - but acknowledges that even if she wins, she "can't [get] my husband's life back".

"I share things that happen in our daily life, as if he still existed," she says. "I often write to him, 'I miss you so much. Are you doing well on the other side?'"

It's a similar story for Mrs Lau, who says she can't go anywhere without seeing her husband.

"Every day, something reminds me of him," she said.

"I still find it very hard to accept that my husband is gone, my home is gone, and so many of my neighbours are gone…. This place was my roots. I never imagined it would also mark an ending for me."

articles.title: Houthis target Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports as strikes escalate
articles.summary: Explosion reported in Sanaa after Saudi air defenses intercept ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh.
articles.body:
Yemen’s Houthi group has struck the port of Jizan on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast as fighting intensifies near the Yemeni city of Taiz.

A Saudi-led military coalition said a Houthi attack on Jizan caused only minor damage and no civilian casualties on Wednesday, adding that “efforts are underway to determine the type of projectile” used.

The spokesman for the coalition, Turki al-Maliki, later said in a statement on X that its forces intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone over Jeddah’s port in Saudi Arabia.

No civilian injuries were reported from falling debris following the interception, he added.

After the coalition’s statement, an explosion was heard in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, according to Al Jazeera’s Nabil al-Yousfi.

The Saudi-led coalition then said its air defences intercepted and destroyed ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh.

The attempted strike on the capital follows a Houthi drone attack on a skyscraper in Riyadh’s financial district on Tuesday, injuring at least 11 people .

The latest incidents mark a further escalation between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia, including strikes from both sides targeting airports, energy facilities and other civilian and economic infrastructure.

The strikes on Saudi Arabian ports come after the Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV reported new Saudi attacks on the port of Hodeidah in Yemen .

Earlier on Wednesday, the Houthis threatened to attack Saudi ports if Hodeidah came under attack.

“The port of Hodeidah handles 90 percent of imported goods into Yemen. If it is closed, it could bring the humanitarian situation to the brink of collapse”, said Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Yemen’s capital, Sanaa.

“Some of Saudi Arabia’s recent attacks at the Port of Hodeidah have targeted storage tanks and cranes used to load and unload shipments”, Mawry said.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces have been battling the Houthis on several fronts, with the army’s spokesman saying 654 strikes have been carried out against the group on Wednesday.

Yemen’s western front has witnessed the heaviest concentration of recent strikes, according to Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali, reporting from Taiz.

Government forces have said air strikes targeted Houthi positions west of Taiz.

“These strikes are part of an intense and sustained wave of air raids that have continued for approximately 72 hours”, Ali said.

“Particular attention is focused on the most significant mountain range overlooking central Taiz: Jabal Saber and its highest peak, Jabal al-Arus. The government says the Houthis want to seize this strategic peak”, she added.

The Houthis said there have been 105 air strikes and missile attacks by the Saudi-led coalition targeting civilian sites in Sanaa and 10 governorates on Wednesday.

articles.body: Rachel Accurso, the progressive children's content creator known as Ms. Rachel, is now turning to explicit language over the conflict in Gaza. "We made enough money for our lives, so I can say anything I want, and I do, like, acknowledge the people who spoke out a long time ago and lost their jobs and didn't have that," Accurso told podcast host Hasan Minhaj. "Like, they were the brave ones. They were amazing. But, like, I'm sorry, that is so f---ed up. I never swear, but I've started swearing because I'm like …" "Go off," Minhaj reacted. ED SHEERAN FACES GROWING BACKLASH AS RADIO STATION BANS SONGS, PROTEST GROUPS RESPOND TO MACKLEMORE'S REMOVAL "I'll see something, and I'll just be like, how is this possible?" she continued. "Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, the U.N. — they're not wrong. B'Tselem, I met with them, the Israeli human rights org. "They're so clear that this is genocide, and you're going to be mad that Macklemore says to end the genocide? That's a great thing to say when there is a genocide." Accurso, who has been an outspoken critic of Israel's actions in Gaza, appeared on Wednesday's installment of the "Hasan Minhaj Doesn't Know" podcast and was asked about her condemnation of music superstar Ed Sheeran, who she accused of caving to pressure after his opening act, Macklemore, was pushed out of Sheeran's tour for chanting "Free Palestine" at a concert. "I see people prioritizing language over children's lives. And I'm not going to play about that," Accurso said. "Because children's lives, Palestinian children's lives matter, and they're still being killed every day. ... "When there's a genocide going on, a genocide which we all have a duty to speak out against — actually, countries have a duty to stop a genocide." MS. Accurso, who has millions of followers on social media with her songs and educational videos for children, has frequently posted about the conflict and condemned celebrities she feels don't use their platforms to advocate for Gazans. Um imigrante de El Salvador que ganhou US$ 1 milhão (R$ 5,8 milhões) na loteria de Massachusetts, nos Estados Unidos , foi preso por agentes do Serviço de Imigração e Controle de Alfândegas (ICE, na sigla em inglês) apenas seis dias depois de receber o prêmio. A prisão ocorreu na terça-feira (24), em East Boston.

Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales havia sido fotografado sorrindo enquanto segurava um cheque gigante com o valor da premiação. A imagem foi publicada pela Loteria de Massachusetts nas redes sociais em 21 de novembro, três dias depois de o prêmio ter sido concedido.

O imigrante era procurado pelas autoridades americanas por causa de uma ordem definitiva de deportação emitida em abril de 2014 , segundo o ICE. Ele entrou ilegalmente nos Estados Unidos em maio de 2013, nas proximidades da cidade de Roma, no Texas.

A agência informou que Velasquez-Morales permanece sob custódia e aguarda a deportação.

"É como se a sorte dele tivesse acabado" , afirmou Micah Bock, diretor-assistente de Relações Públicas do ICE, em comunicado enviado ao jornal britânico Daily Mail.

Velasquez-Morales ganhou o prêmio no jogo de raspadinha "$2,000,000 50X Cashword", da Loteria de Massachusetts. Ele comprou um bilhete de US$ 10 (R$ 58) em um mercado de East Boston, bairro onde mora e onde acabou sendo preso.

Segundo a organização, o imigrante acertou 11 palavras logo no primeiro bilhete que raspou.

Ele optou por receber o prêmio à vista. Nessa modalidade, o valor pago é de US$ 650 mil (cerca de R$ 3,7 milhões) , antes da cobrança dos impostos, em vez dos US$ 1 milhão anunciados como prêmio.

Agente do ICE durante operação em Mineápolis, em 18 de janeiro de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS/Seth Herald

Imigrante entrou ilegalmente nos EUA em 2013

De acordo com a nota à imprensa do ICE, Velasquez-Morales atravessou ilegalmente a fronteira americana em 2013, perto de Roma, no Texas. Na ocasião, agentes da Patrulha de Fronteira emitiram uma notificação para que ele comparecesse perante um juiz de imigração.

A agência afirmou que ele foi liberado para permanecer nos Estados Unidos e recebeu uma lista de prestadores de serviços jurídicos gratuitos. Segundo o ICE, isso ocorreu durante o governo do então presidente Barack Obama.

Em abril de 2014, um juiz de imigração determinou que ele fosse deportado. Mesmo assim, Velasquez-Morales continuou no país, segundo as autoridades.

David Wesling, diretor interino do escritório de Operações de Fiscalização e Remoção do ICE em Boston, afirmou ao jornal Boston Herald que o imigrante ignorou a ordem judicial por mais de 12 anos.

O ICE também publicou uma mensagem sobre a prisão na rede social X, acompanhada da fotografia de Velasquez-Morales com o cheque milionário.

"Bem-vindos à loteria do ERO Boston! Aqui, imigrantes em situação irregular e políticos que protegem essas pessoas não têm sorte, enquanto os cidadãos que respeitam a lei da Nova Inglaterra são sempre os vencedores!", escreveu a agência.

articles.title: Prospera chega à 4ª edição com mais de mil atendimentos em São Pedro da Aldeia | G1
articles.standfirst: Promovido pela Prolagos e pelo Instituto Aegea, evento ofereceu serviços gratuitos de saúde, cidadania e bem-estar.
articles.summary: Promovido pela Prolagos e pelo Instituto Aegea, evento ofereceu serviços gratuitos de saúde, cidadania e bem-estar.
articles.body:
O evento mobilizou mais de 100 voluntários e ofereceu atividades para todas as idades — Foto: Ascom Prolagos

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Saúde, cidadania, lazer e solidariedade marcaram a quarta edição do Prospera, realizada no dia 7 de novembro, em São Pedro da Aldeia. A iniciativa transformou o CIEP 272, no bairro São João, em um grande espaço de inclusão e prestação de serviços gratuitos, reunindo centenas de moradores. Durante a programação, profissionais prestaram orientações, voluntários acolheram os participantes e famílias circularam entre os diferentes espaços, em uma mobilização voltada ao bem-estar da comunidade.

Promovido pela Prolagos e pelo Instituto Aegea, o evento mobilizou mais de 100 voluntários e ofereceu atividades para pessoas de todas as idades. Ao todo, 1.058 atendimentos foram realizados durante as quatro horas de programação, reforçando a importância da iniciativa para ampliar o acesso da população a serviços essenciais.

Entre os moradores que participaram da ação estava a técnica de saúde bucal Fabiana Sousa. Com a rotina de trabalho durante a semana, ela encontrou no Prospera a oportunidade de buscar atendimento presencial da Prolagos, esclarecer dúvidas sobre sua conta de água e regularizar pendências com a concessionária. Além da facilidade de acesso ao serviço, Fabiana destacou a organização do evento.

"Durante a semana, por causa do trabalho, fica difícil conseguir ir até a loja da Prolagos. Quando soube que teria atendimento aqui, aproveitei a oportunidade para resolver minhas pendências. Fui muito bem atendida e fiquei encantada com toda essa estrutura. É muito bom ter tantos serviços reunidos em um só lugar", contou Fabiana.

O espaço dedicado à saúde e ao bem-estar esteve entre os pontos de maior movimentação do evento, oferecendo mini check-up, consultas clínicas, exames de vista, aferição de pressão e glicose, atendimento odontológico, fisioterapia e massagens rápidas.

A programação também contou com a participação do Ministério da Saúde, que promoveu a atualização das cadernetas de vacinação. Durante o evento, o personagem Zé Gotinha circulou pelo espaço, incentivando a imunização de crianças e adultos. Em uma das salas do CIEP, o Ministério organizou uma roda de conversa sobre o Novembro Azul, campanha que reforça a importância da prevenção e dos cuidados com a saúde masculina.

A Secretaria Municipal de Saúde disponibilizou vacinação antirrábica para cães, enquanto a Patrulha Maria da Penha promoveu uma palestra de conscientização sobre a violência contra a mulher.

Na área de beleza e autocuidado, os atendimentos também atraíram moradores interessados em renovar o visual. Gabrielle Soares, moradora do bairro, aproveitou o trabalho das trancistas e conheceu outros serviços disponíveis, incluindo o corte de cabelo.

"Eu gostei muito! Fui super bem atendida, aproveitei para fazer minhas tranças e ainda passei por outros espaços, como o de corte de cabelo. É muito bom ter uma ação assim perto de casa, com tantas opções para a gente aproveitar", destacou Gabrielle.

As crianças estão se divertindo — Foto: Ascom Prolagos

A animação também tomou conta do espaço reservado às crianças. O Prolaguito, mascote da concessionária, participou da festa e garantiu momentos de diversão ao lado dos pequenos. A recreação contou com pula-pula, pintura facial, distribuição de pipoca e algodão-doce, fazendo do Prospera um programa para toda a família. Enquanto as crianças brincavam, os adultos aproveitavam os serviços de cidadania, como orientações sobre o CadÚnico, emissão e parcelamento de IPTU, agendamento para isenção de documentos pela Fundação Leão XIII e atendimentos da Ouvidoria da Secretaria Municipal de Saúde. Também foram oferecidos serviços comerciais da Prolagos e da Enel, além de orientações da Auto Viação Salineira.

A programação incluiu ainda atividades de educação e sustentabilidade, com o Laboratório Móvel da Prolagos, ações do Projeto Albatroz, a Van Experience da Enel, doação de mudas e orientações sobre cursos da Firjan e da Universidade Veiga de Almeida. Demonstração de confeitaria com degustação, promovida pela Vivian Festas, e distribuição de brindes do Grupo Profarma também fizeram parte das atrações.

O evento abriu espaço para empreendedores locais, que montaram barracas para apresentar e comercializar seus produtos. Além de ampliar as opções para os visitantes, a iniciativa proporcionou uma oportunidade de divulgação dos pequenos negócios e geração de renda extra.

Voluntariado que faz a diferença - Por trás de cada atendimento, a dedicação dos voluntários ajudou a transformar o evento em uma experiência de acolhimento. Colaboradores da Prolagos e integrantes das instituições parceiras se dividiram entre a organização dos espaços, a orientação ao público e o apoio às equipes responsáveis pelos serviços.

Para Paolla de Jesus, colaboradora do setor Administrativo da Prolagos, a experiência foi especialmente marcante.

"Foi uma experiência muito especial. Desde cedo, muitas pessoas chegaram procurando o exame de vista, e eu fiquei responsável por organizar a distribuição das senhas. A gente percebe como um atendimento pode fazer a diferença para alguém. Ver a alegria e a gratidão das pessoas faz todo o esforço valer a pena. Foi um sábado que vou guardar com muito carinho", afirmou Paolla.

Para a coordenadora de Responsabilidade Social da Prolagos, Aline Araújo, o envolvimento dos voluntários e das instituições parceiras foi fundamental para o sucesso da iniciativa.

"O Prospera é uma grande mobilização de pessoas que acreditam no poder da solidariedade e do trabalho coletivo. Ver a comunidade chegando desde cedo, as famílias aproveitando os serviços e nossos voluntários tão envolvidos mostra a importância dessa iniciativa. Mais do que oferecer atendimentos gratuitos, queremos proporcionar acolhimento, acesso a oportunidades e momentos que façam a diferença na vida das pessoas", destacou Aline.

Realizado simultaneamente em diferentes unidades da Aegea, o Prospera integra as iniciativas de responsabilidade social do grupo e reforça o compromisso da Prolagos com o desenvolvimento das comunidades da Região dos Lagos.

Ao todo, 1.058 atendimentos foram realizados durante as quatro horas de programação no CIEP 272 — Foto: Ascom Prolagos

articles.title: Socorristas voluntários são impedidos de atuar no RS | G1
articles.standfirst: Instituições 'Anjos do Asfalto' e 'Corpo Voluntário de Socorro e Resgate' estão proibidas de atuar em Gravataí. Secretaria de Saúde alega falta de regulação médica nos atendimentos.
articles.summary: Socorristas voluntários de Gravataí são impedidos de atuar após ações do Ministério Público que buscam regularizar o atendimento pré-hospitalar e o vínculo com o SUS.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

O Ministério Público do Rio Grande do Sul (MPRS) entrou com duas ações civis públicas para regularizar o atendimento pré-hospitalar prestado por grupos voluntários em Gravataí , na Região Metropolitana de Porto Alegre .

A medida ocorre após a prefeitura suspender as atividades de duas instituições de socorro da cidade , alegando irregularidades e falta de regulação médica nos serviços.

Os atendimentos do grupo Anjos do Asfalto estão paralisados desde a semana passada. Já o Corpo Voluntário de Socorro e Resgate (CVSR) teve as atividades suspensas nesta terça-feira (24). Juntas, as duas instituições somam cerca de 270 socorristas voluntários e cinco ambulâncias , que agora estão impedidos de atuar.

De acordo com o município, a interdição é resultado de irregularidades apontadas em fiscalizações, como a ausência de regulação médica nos atendimentos pré-hospitalares . A prefeitura defende que o serviço precisa seguir as normas técnicas e legais que regulamentam a rede de urgência e emergência.

"Nós não somos contra o trabalho voluntário, não. Enquanto Saúde, nós também queremos que muitos voluntários atuem na nossa rede, mas é preciso que o critério técnico seja resguardado", afirma o secretário de Saúde de Gravataí, Régis Fonseca.

A diretoria do CVSR contesta os motivos apresentados pela prefeitura . A presidente da instituição, Ana Konrath, declarou que a equipe não pratica atos que envolvam procedimentos invasivos .

"Se nós voltarmos às ruas, a gente pode ser autuado com uma multa que pode ir até R$ 50 mil, e aqui é uma instituição que é 100% voluntária", disse. Segundo ela, a perda dos dois grupos para a cidade será "incalculável" .

Com cerca de 200 voluntários, o "Anjos do Asfalto" informou que recebeu a decisão de interdição total com preocupação e que vai buscar esclarecimentos junto aos órgãos competentes .

As ações civis públicas movidas pelo MP contra a prefeitura e as instituições têm o objetivo de regularizar o atendimento , estabelecer um plano de ação e criar formas de integração com o Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS).

Uma das alternativas avaliadas é buscar vínculo com o Corpo de Bombeiros, o que permitiria aos grupos continuar operando dentro de outro enquadramento legal.

A interdição não significa que Gravataí ficará sem serviço de emergência . O secretário de Saúde explicou a estrutura atual do município.

"Nós temos hoje no município duas ambulâncias de suporte básico, muito suporte avançado, cumprindo o critério populacional e nós estaremos avaliando [...] a possibilidade até de ampliação das unidades do Samu, se for necessário", disse o secretário.

Enquanto o futuro das instituições depende de encaminhamentos administrativos e judiciais, moradores que já precisaram do serviço temem ficar sem assistência.

Para a porteira Maria Jurema Melo, a cidade vai "virar um caos" sem os grupos. A cabeleireira Lorena Schumacher Madalena também criticou a paralisação do serviço.

"Quantas pessoas dependem deste atendimento? [...] O prefeito tem que dar um jeito nisso, porque as pessoas precisam", cobra.

articles.title: Brasileira presa na China por tráfico estava sumida há 2 meses | G1
articles.standfirst: Mãe de três filhos, Lucimara Caroline Norberto Ferreira, de 32 anos, trabalhava na área de serviços gerais de uma indústria farmacêutica antes de viajar para o exterior.
articles.summary: Brasileira presa na China, Lucimara Caroline Ferreira estava desaparecida há dois meses e é investigada por suspeita de tráfico no aeroporto de Kunming.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Lucimara Caroline Norberto Ferreira, de 32 anos, moradora de Pouso Alegre , no Sul de Minas, foi presa na China sob suspeita de envolvimento com tráfico de drogas . Mãe de três filhos, ela trabalhava havia cinco meses na área de serviços gerais de uma indústria farmacêutica antes de viajar para o exterior.

A prisão foi confirmada pelo Ministério das Relações Exteriores (Itamaraty), após a família passar mais de dois meses sem notícias dela.

Segundo a mãe, Julmara Clementino Norberto, Lucimara havia informado que viajaria para a Europa. A família perdeu o contato com ela em 15 de agosto.

“A última vez que falei com ela, perguntei onde estava. Ela disse que em Paris”, contou.

Família procurava por moradora de Pouso Alegre desaparecida há dois meses e meio após viagem à Europa — Foto: Reprodução EPTV

Julmara afirmou que não sabe o que a filha foi fazer na Ásia. “Ela foi encontrada na China e está presa suspeita. Está passando por uma investigação. Graças a Deus conseguimos encontrá-la”, disse a mãe.

Lucimara é mãe de três crianças. Os dois filhos mais novos, de 6 e 7 anos, estão sob os cuidados da avó materna. Já o filho mais velho, de 12 anos, está com o pai.

A mãe descreveu a filha como uma pessoa amorosa e dedicada aos filhos.

"Ela trabalhava como faxineira há cinco meses. É amorosa, boa, cuidava dos filhos. Levava sempre para passear", afirmou.

Conforme o Itamaraty, Lucimara foi detida em 18 de agosto, no Aeroporto de Kunming, na província de Yunnan. Ela permanece no Centro de Detenção de Kunming enquanto aguarda a conclusão das investigações.

Brasileira é presa na China sob suspeita de tráfico de drogas; mulher ficou desaparecida por 2 meses — Foto: Arquivo Família

O Ministério informou que, em casos de detenção criminal com investigações em andamento, as autoridades chinesas não permitem contato telefônico com a pessoa detida.

O Consulado-Geral do Brasil em Chengdu acompanha o caso e mantém contato com as autoridades locais.

Ao g1, o advogado de defesa de Lucimara, Telêmaco Marrace, afirmou que ainda não há confirmação do envolvimento da brasileira com o tráfico de drogas.

"Ainda estão investigando. Então, seria precipitado dizer que ela teria prisão perpétua ou pena de morte, porque na China, para esse tipo de caso, principalmente brasileiros ou estrangeiros que são pegos lá, existe a prisão temporária", explicou.

O advogado afirmou que Lucimara poderá permanecer detida por um período e, posteriormente, ser extraditada para o Brasil, conforme o andamento do caso.

articles.summary: Apostas podem ser feitas até as 20h em lotéricas ou pela internet.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

O concurso 3.091 da Mega-Sena pode pagar um prêmio de R$ 75 milhões para os apostadores que acertarem as seis dezenas. O sorteio ocorre às 21h desta quinta-feira (26), em São Paulo.

No concurso da última terça (24), ninguém levou a faixa principal.

O g1 transmite todos os sorteios das Loterias Caixa, ao vivo . A transmissão começa momentos antes de cada dia de concursos, no site e no canal do g1 no YouTube .

A aposta mínima para a Mega-Sena custa R$ 6 e pode ser realizada também pela internet – saiba como fazer a sua aposta online .

Volante da Mega-Sena — Foto: Ana Marin/g1

As apostas podem ser realizadas até as 20h (horário de Brasília) em qualquer lotérica do país ou por meio do site e aplicativo Loterias Caixa, disponíveis em smartphones, computadores e outros dispositivos.

Já os bolões digitais poderão ser comprados até as 20h30, exclusivamente pelo portal Loterias Online e pelo aplicativo.

Ainda segundo a Caixa, para os sorteios realizados aos domingos as apostas simples podem ser efetuadas até as 22h de sábado por meio das unidades lotéricas, pelo Portal Loterias Caixa e do aplicativo Loterias Caixa.

A comercialização dos Bolões Caixa nos canais eletrônicos, nesse caso, acontece até às 10h45 do domingo, quinze minutos antes da realização dos sorteios.

O pagamento da aposta online pode ser realizado via PIX, cartão de crédito ou pelo internet banking, para correntistas da Caixa. É preciso ter 18 anos ou mais para participar.

A probabilidade de vencer em cada concurso varia de acordo com o número de dezenas jogadas e do tipo de aposta realizada. Para um jogo simples, com apenas seis dezenas, que custa R$ 6, a probabilidade de ganhar o prêmio milionário é de 1 em 50.063.860, segundo a Caixa.

Já para uma aposta com 20 dezenas (limite máximo), com o preço de R$ 232.560,00, a probabilidade de acertar o prêmio é de 1 em 1.292, ainda de acordo com a instituição.

Trata-se de um levantamento inédito sobre o panorama e os avanços das 31 maiores facções brasileiras nas últimas duas décadas. O recorte temporal deste trabalho coincide com os 20 anos do chamado "salve geral" do PCC, que paralisou São Paulo, e de uma série de ataques coordenados do Comando Vermelho, no Rio. E o que se vê hoje são organizações que multiplicam suas práticas criminosas para além do tráfico de drogas – muitas delas atuam como milícias infiltradas na economia local – e que se expandem por todo o território, inclusive para fora do país.
