articles.title: Chuva de até 110 mm pode provocar alagamentos e inundações em SP, RJ, ES e MG nesta quinta-feira; veja a previsão do tempo | G1
articles.standfirst: Litoral norte paulista e regiões do Rio de Janeiro, Espírito Santo e Minas Gerais devem concentrar os maiores volumes de chuva, segundo a Climatempo. Centro-Oeste também terá risco de temporais, enquanto temperaturas devem cair ligeiramente no Sul e em parte do Sudeste.
articles.summary: Litoral norte paulista e regiões do Rio de Janeiro, Espírito Santo e Minas Gerais devem concentrar os maiores volumes de chuva, segundo a Climatempo. Centro-Oeste também terá risco de temporais, enquanto temperaturas devem cair ligeiramente no Sul e em parte do Sudeste.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

A chuva pode chegar a 110 milímetros em áreas do Sudeste nesta quinta-feira (26), com risco de alagamentos, inundações e rajadas fortes de vento . Segundo a Climatempo, os maiores volumes são esperados no litoral norte de São Paulo, no Rio de Janeiro, incluindo a capital e o norte fluminense, no sul do Espírito Santo e em parte do Vale do Rio Doce, em Minas Gerais.

Nessas localidades, os acumulados podem variar entre 80 e 110 milímetros . A combinação de áreas de instabilidade com as características do relevo favorece a formação de nuvens carregadas, aumentando o potencial para temporais e chuva volumosa.

O mau tempo também deve atingir o Centro-Oeste , onde o calor e a umidade mantêm as condições favoráveis à ocorrência de pancadas intensas. No Norte, Rondônia e Acre estão entre os estados com previsão de chuva forte. Já no Nordeste, as instabilidades devem se concentrar no litoral do Rio Grande do Norte, da Paraíba e de Pernambuco.

Apesar da chuva, não há previsão de frio intenso. A mudança na direção dos ventos deve transportar ar um pouco mais frio para São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro e estados do Sul, provocando uma redução moderada nas temperaturas.

Sudeste concentra os maiores volumes de chuva

O litoral norte de São Paulo e o Vale do Paraíba estão entre as áreas com maior risco de temporais nesta quinta-feira. A chuva pode ocorrer com forte intensidade, especialmente no litoral, onde os acumulados elevados aumentam a possibilidade de alagamentos e inundações.

No Rio de Janeiro, as instabilidades devem atingir diferentes regiões do estado , incluindo a capital e o norte fluminense. Os volumes podem chegar a 110 milímetros em algumas localidades, com possibilidade de ventos fortes durante as pancadas.

O sul do Espírito Santo e parte do Vale do Rio Doce, em Minas Gerais, também estão entre as áreas que exigem atenção . Nessas regiões, o relevo contribui para intensificar a formação de nuvens carregadas e favorecer volumes elevados de precipitação.

Em outras áreas de Minas Gerais e do Espírito Santo, a previsão também indica risco de temporais, embora os maiores acumulados estejam concentrados nas localidades próximas à faixa de instabilidade mais intensa.

As temperaturas devem apresentar uma leve queda em São Paulo e no Rio de Janeiro, devido à mudança na direção dos ventos . A redução, porém, não será suficiente para provocar frio intenso.

risco de temporais, quinta-feira — Foto: Climatempo

Sul: temperaturas mais amenas; RS ainda enfrenta consequências de temporal

No Sul, a entrada de ar mais frio deve provocar uma redução nas temperaturas nesta quinta-feira. A queda, no entanto, será moderada, sem previsão de frio intenso.

A mudança no tempo ocorre enquanto o Rio Grande do Sul ainda enfrenta as consequências das tempestades dos últimos dias . Em Tupanciretã, atingida por um temporal na sexta-feira (20), o Ministério da Saúde enviou nesta quarta (25) dois kits emergenciais com medicamentos e insumos para reforçar a assistência à população. Juntos, os materiais têm capacidade para atender até 1,5 mil pessoas por mês.

Equipes da Força Nacional do Sistema Único de Saúde (FN-SUS) também apoiaram a retomada dos atendimentos em duas Unidades Básicas de Saúde (UBS) e a ampliação da assistência por meio de unidades móveis, que realizam cerca de 90 atendimentos.

Centro-Oeste: temporais por causa do calor e da umidade

Praticamente todo o Centro-Oeste deve permanecer sob risco de temporais nesta quinta-feira. As temperaturas elevadas, combinadas à umidade disponível na atmosfera, favorecem a formação de nuvens carregadas e pancadas de chuva que podem ser intensas.

O sul de Mato Grosso do Sul está entre as áreas que exigem atenção, devido ao deslocamento de instabilidades pela região.

As pancadas podem ocorrer acompanhadas de descargas elétricas e rajadas de vento, com possibilidade de chuva forte em diferentes localidades.

Norte: chuva forte em Rondônia e no Acre

Na região Norte, Rondônia e Acre devem registrar pancadas de chuva que podem ganhar intensidade ao longo desta quinta-feira.

A atuação de áreas de instabilidade sobre os dois estados favorece a formação de nuvens carregadas, mantendo as condições para chuva forte em diferentes localidades.

Nordeste: pancadas intensas no litoral de três estados

No Nordeste, a chuva deve se concentrar em áreas do litoral do Rio Grande do Norte, da Paraíba e de Pernambuco, com possibilidade de pancadas fortes nesta quinta-feira.

A instabilidade está associada à circulação de ventos nas camadas mais altas da atmosfera, que favorece a formação de nuvens de chuva sobre essa faixa do litoral.

Diferentemente das áreas do Sudeste, onde há previsão de acumulados elevados, a chuva no litoral nordestino deve ocorrer em episódios localizados, que podem ser intensos, mas de curta duração.

articles.title: Escolher cuba e monocomando em conjunto evita erros na bancada  | G1
articles.standfirst: Medidas, tipo de instalação e alcance da bica ajudam a definir uma combinação mais funcional para a cozinha.
articles.summary: Medidas, tipo de instalação e alcance da bica ajudam a definir uma combinação mais funcional para a cozinha.
articles.body:
Uma cuba pode ter as dimensões ideais para a rotina. Um monocomando pode oferecer mobilidade e bom alcance. Ainda assim, escolher os dois separadamente não significa que funcionarão bem juntos na bancada.

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Na cozinha, proporção, profundidade, posição do metal e área livre para uso precisam ser analisadas como um conjunto. Uma bica com alcance inadequado pode direcionar a água muito próxima da borda. Uma cuba grande demais pode ocupar a área prevista para preparo. Até o acionamento do monocomando precisa ter espaço para funcionar sem encontrar parede, frontão ou outros elementos.

Cuba, monocomando e bancada precisam ser avaliados em conjunto para que dimensões, alcance da água e área disponível funcionem bem na rotina — Foto: Acervo Vilarejo

A medida da cuba interfere em toda a bancada

A Cuba Michigan 64x38, da DAX , é uma opção de sobrepor em aço inox com acabamento fosco. Suas dimensões externas são de aproximadamente 64 por 38 centímetros, o que já mostra por que a escolha precisa acontecer antes da execução definitiva da bancada.

A Cuba Michigan 64x38, da DAX, mostra como as dimensões da peça precisam ser consideradas junto com profundidade da bancada e espaço disponível para preparo — Foto: Acervo Vilarejo

Não basta verificar se a cuba cabe. É importante observar quanto da bancada continuará livre, onde ficará o metal e se haverá espaço confortável entre a peça, a parede e outros elementos próximos.

O tipo de instalação também interfere. Como a Michigan é de sobrepor, a relação entre recorte e borda é diferente daquela encontrada em modelos de embutir. A DAX orienta que a preparação do tampo e a instalação sigam as medidas técnicas do produto.

Alcance da bica importa tanto quanto a altura

Depois da cuba, entra outra medida importante. Onde a água vai cair?

O Monocomando Thelon Bica Móvel Redondo, da DAX, foi desenvolvido para cozinhas e possui bica giratória em 360 graus e arejador articulado. Essas características aumentam a mobilidade sobre a cuba, mas também reforçam a necessidade de avaliar sua posição na bancada.

O Monocomando Thelon, da DAX, possui bica móvel com giro de 360 graus e mostra como alcance e posicionamento interferem diretamente no uso da cuba — Foto: Acervo Vilarejo

A saída de água precisa encontrar uma região confortável da cuba. Quando fica muito próxima da borda, pode favorecer respingos. Quando a proporção entre bica e cuba não é adequada, tarefas simples como lavar uma panela ou encher um recipiente podem se tornar menos práticas.

Também é necessário conferir a área necessária para movimentar a alavanca e a distância em relação ao frontão ou à parede. A DAX indica instalação de mesa para o Thelon e recomenda um furo de aproximadamente 37 milímetros para seus monocomandos de cozinha e lavatório.

O desenho da bancada começa antes do recorte

Por isso, definir primeiro a cuba e deixar o monocomando para depois pode limitar a escolha. O contrário também acontece.

Antes de executar os recortes, vale reunir as fichas técnicas dos dois produtos e conferir largura e profundidade da cuba, profundidade total da bancada, posição do furo, alcance da bica e área necessária para o acionamento.

Essa conferência é ainda mais importante em bancadas compactas, próximas a janelas ou com pouco espaço entre a cuba e o frontão.

O atendimento especializado da Vilarejo pode ajudar a colocar essas informações lado a lado antes da compra. Com medidas e planta da bancada em mãos, fica mais fácil avaliar se os dois produtos realmente funcionam juntos no espaço disponível.

DAX conecta desenvolvimento de produto e experiência no varejo

A DAX é uma marca exclusiva da Vilarejo em sua região de atuação e foi desenvolvida por meio da Associação Casa Vip, iniciativa formada por redes especializadas no segmento de acabamentos. A presença do grupo em mais de 120 lojas pelo Brasil aproxima o desenvolvimento dos produtos das necessidades percebidas diariamente nos pontos de venda. A Casa Vip identifica a DAX como uma de suas marcas próprias voltadas a metais, cubas, louças e outros produtos para cozinhas, banheiros e lavabos.

Na bancada da cozinha, essa variedade só entrega seu melhor resultado quando as peças são especificadas em conjunto.

Um bom produto escolhido isoladamente pode não ser a melhor combinação. Compatibilidade é o que transforma duas boas escolhas em uma bancada que realmente funciona no dia a dia.

articles.title: Calor: 5 em cada 9 moradores da Maré dizem passar mal em casa | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento ouviu mais de 1,6 mil pessoas e identificou problemas de ventilação e desconforto térmico. Outro estudo apontou que 70% das medições de poluição ficaram acima do recomendado pela OMS.
articles.summary: Levantamento ouviu mais de 1,6 mil pessoas e identificou problemas de ventilação e desconforto térmico. Outro estudo apontou que 70% das medições de poluição ficaram acima do recom
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Cinco em cada nove moradores do Complexo da Maré, na Zona Norte do Rio, afirmam passar mal dentro de casa por causa das altas temperaturas . O dado faz parte de uma pesquisa sobre os impactos das mudanças climáticas na saúde de moradores de favelas, realizada pela Redes da Maré em parceria com o Insper, a Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ) e a Fundação Oswaldo Cruz (Fiocruz).

O levantamento ouviu mais de 1,6 mil pessoas e mostrou que o calor afeta diretamente as condições de moradia na região. Segundo a pesquisa, 60% dos entrevistados consideram suas casas muito quentes e 65% afirmam viver em locais sem ventilação adequada.

Os resultados reforçam a percepção dos moradores de que o calor é mais intenso na Maré e mostram como as condições de moradia e a falta de infraestrutura podem agravar os efeitos das altas temperaturas.

Cinco em cada nove moradores da Maré dizem passar mal em casa por causa do calor, aponta pesquisa — Foto: Reprodução TV Globo

Outro estudo, desenvolvido pela Redes da Maré em parceria com o Instituto de Tecnologia de Massachusetts (MIT), dos Estados Unidos, a Secretaria Municipal de Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação e a Firjan, investigou a temperatura e a qualidade do ar no território.

Durante o último verão, moradores e pesquisadores circularam pelas ruas da Maré com equipamentos conhecidos como “polvos”, sensores utilizados para medir a temperatura e a poluição do ar.

As medições indicaram que 70% dos registros de poluição apontaram níveis acima do recomendado pela Organização Mundial da Saúde (OMS). Na medição com a maior média registrada, a concentração chegou a seis vezes o limite indicado pela entidade.

O estudo também identificou maior presença de calor e poluição em casas onde vivem famílias mais pobres.

Para Kenny Knuppe, articulador da Redes da Maré, os resultados confirmam uma realidade conhecida por quem vive no território.

“A gente que mora na maré tem consciência que a Maré é mais quente. O pessoal que não conhece muito bem foi entender que a Maré é mais quente depois dos estudos, mas a gente já sabe que aqui é mais quente há muito tempo. A gente vê que não tem arvores, pontos cheios de lixo”

Diferenças de temperatura dentro da própria Maré

Os estudos apontaram que a Maré funciona como uma ilha de calor , com temperaturas acima da média. Mas a situação não é igual em todas as áreas do complexo. Há pontos onde a combinação de fatores urbanos torna o ambiente ainda mais quente.

É o caso da região conhecida como Favela da Galinha. A verticalização das construções, a pouca presença de árvores, a proximidade de um lixão e a localização entre vias expressas contribuem para elevar a temperatura.

O aposentado Fábio Afonso mora na região há sete anos. Ele se interessou pelo monitoramento depois de ver um funcionário da Redes da Maré circulando com um dos equipamentos.

“Eu me interessei porque vejo que o ar é ruim, pela proximidade da Linha Vermelha, Linha Amarela. Agora isso aqui é o xodó, sempre to testando o ar pra ver se o ar ta melhorando”.

Morador transforma área de lixo em horta

Enquanto as políticas públicas para melhorar as condições ambientais não chegam, Fábio tenta contribuir com pequenas iniciativas. Ele aproveitou um espaço que antes era usado para o descarte de lixo e começou a plantar mudas e árvores frutíferas.

"Eu comecei com mudinhas de planta (...) Eu passo próximo de uma casa, vejo um jardim, chamo a moradora, peço um galhozinho. Comecei assim"

O espaço já produziu milho e quiabo, que foram colhidos e compartilhados com outros moradores.

Morador transforma área de lixo em horta. — Foto: Reprodução TV Globo

Fábio diz que percebeu uma melhora no ambiente desde que começou a plantar, mesmo que em pequena escala.

"Eu sei que é pouco planta, mas um poucadinho já melhorou o ar, depois que eu comecei"

Como as casas são muito próximas, ele evita espécies com raízes grandes, que poderiam comprometer as construções. A ideia é continuar cultivando plantas e árvores frutíferas que se adaptem ao espaço.

"Eu gostaria de plantar mangueira, cajá... mas não posso plantar arvore. Aqui dentro não tem como porque as casas são muito próximas, raiz grande, pode dar rachadura. Bom, vou plantar planta que não tem raiz muito forte. Mamão, acerola, maracujá, tangerina, goiaba"

"Ao mesmo tempo que dá fruto, vai melhorando nosso ar"

Pesquisas querem orientar políticas públicas

Os estudos foram desenvolvidos para produzir dados sobre os efeitos do calor e da poluição na vida dos moradores e contribuir para a formulação de políticas públicas voltadas às favelas.

O secretário municipal de Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação, Gabriel Medina, afirmou que os diagnósticos podem ajudar no planejamento de intervenções urbanas previstas para comunidades como a Maré e a Rocinha.

"A ideia é informar políticas públicas federais. A gente está em curso com o Pac da Rocinha e da Mare, já com grandes transformações previstas pra essas comunidades e esses diagnósticos podem tb ajudar no planejamento dessas intervenções urbanas (....) que é olhar pra favela como lugar de produção de dados e também de transformações pra melhorar a vida daquela população".

Para Carolina Dias, coordenadora da Redes da Maré, a produção de conhecimento sobre o território é uma forma de cobrar mudanças e garantir direitos.

"As organizações territoriais investem na pesquisa justamente pq a gente quer incidir nas políticas públicas, a gente produz o conhecimento e agora que a gente tem esse conhecimento a gente quer que isso seja revertido numa melhor qualidade de vida e na garantia de direitos pra quem vive nesse território".

articles.title: Stalking law simplified to become one offence
articles.summary: The new stalking offence will be introduced after a review found existing legislation was confusing.
articles.body:
A new standalone offence of stalking is to be created in England and Wales after a review found the law regarding the crime was "cluttered and confused" - but the maximum sentence will not be increased.

Specific stalking offences were introduced in 2012 but the underlying offence of harassment had to be established, and additional factors such as fear or distress proven, for it to be considered stalking.

A review was ordered by the government last year, led by Richard Wright KC, who prosecuted the man who stalked and murdered Alice Ruggles in Gateshead in 2016.

Victims of stalking have welcomed the change in law but said they were disappointed not all the recommendations have been adopted.

Katherine, from Newcastle, whose former partner was arrested 28 times for stalking her, welcomed the government's decision to introduce one stalking offence instead of two.

"I'm pleased about that one because my ex was charged with [the lesser offence] of stalking without fear to start with and I was terrified," she said.

"Anyone who's been stalked knows how terrifying it is, so that one [without fear] was just pointless."

But her ex had resumed his behaviour after being sentenced to three years and four months in prison, and she criticised the length of jail terms given to stalkers, which she described as "an absolute joke and an insult to the victims".

Ashley, from Washington, in Tyne and Wear, was also disappointed the maximum sentence would not be increased.

"Stalking can have a devastating and lifelong impact on victims and their families," she said.

"It affects your confidence, independence and ability to feel safe, even long after the relationship has ended and the perpetrator has been sentenced."

Of the two current offences, only the more serious charge, which requires proof of fear of violence on at least two occasions, can be tried in the Crown Court, where the potential sentence is greater.

The government has accepted the introduction of a single offence for stalking that can be tried in either Crown or magistrates' court and described it as the "biggest shake-up of stalking laws in more than a decade".

But documents seen by the BBC show ministers rejected Wright's proposal to raise the maximum sentence from 10 to 14 years.

Ministers said the average sentence for the more serious stalking offence in the year to March was 18.6 months, suggesting the existing maximum was not being fully used.

Safeguarding minister Satvir Kaur said: "It's really important that victims know that we are holding perpetrators to account and feeling the full force of the law.

"The average sentences being given aren't good enough."

She said judges were already able to jail stalkers for 10 years so it was better to work with them to make sure they used the powers available to them than "changing the goal posts" on the maximum sentence.

The review was submitted to ministers earlier this year and last month Alice Ruggles's father, Clive Ruggles, said victims of stalking would be at greater risk of dying if the government failed to publish and act on the recommendations.

Alice was killed in her Gateshead flat by her ex-boyfriend Trimaan Dhillon, who was found guilty of murdering the 24-year-old and jailed for 22 years.

Her family has campaigned for better recognition of stalking and improvements in how it is tackled.

Reacting to Thursday's announcement, Alice's parents said they "welcomed" the report and recommendations.

They added they were "heartened" that the response "endorses the need for a single stalking offence that focuses on the perpetrator's behaviour and removes the onus on police and the CPS to prove the impact upon the victim".

Wright's review concluded confusion between stalking and harassment laws could contribute to failures in identifying and prosecuting the crime.

A previous investigation into police handling of stalking found three in every 20 stalking crimes examined had been incorrectly recorded as other offences, including harassment.

The review also recommends removing the need for victims to demonstrate actual fear or serious disruption to their lives for a stalking offence to be established.

Wright argues this would better protect victims who were unaware they are being secretly followed or monitored.

The government said it would explore introducing such a test but had not yet committed to its inclusion in the new offence, although Kaur said she was "sick and tired of it being the onus on the victim".

The review called for more consistent police investigations and greater use of specialist interventions to protect victims.

It also raised concerns about stalkers using applications to change protective orders as a means of maintaining contact with, or control over, victims.

Wright suggests additional safeguards, including requiring court permission before certain applications can proceed and ensuring victims can make representations.

The government acknowledged the problem but said it needed to explore the suggestions further.

Ashley, who was stalked by her former husband Jason Howe using an AirTag to track her movements, said she was "genuinely disappointed" by this response.

Howe was jailed for three years and four months in March last year for stalking and controlling or coercive behaviour.

But Ashley later discovered a restraining order designed to protect her had been amended, without her being consulted, allowing him to use a road through an exclusion zone near her home.

"A restraining order is supposed to protect victims, not provide another opportunity for perpetrators to maintain control," she said.

The government has decided not to adopt a recommendation that would allow previously convicted stalkers to face a new stalking prosecution after just one further incident involving the same victim.

Instead, in previously announced legislation which comes into force on Thursday, courts will now be able to use stalking protection orders in cases of both conviction or acquittal.

"These orders can be in place for as long as is needed," Kaur said.

The government said it would introduce the new legislation as soon as parliamentary time allowed, but had not set a date.

articles.title: BBC launches partnership with Met Office for weather coverage
articles.summary: The corporation says the deal will deliver more regional, digital and 10-day forecasts to audiences.
articles.body:
The BBC has said it will offer more regional, digital and 10-day weather forecasts under a new partnership with the Met Office, which begins on Thursday.

The collaboration, announced last year, aims to bring together the Met Office's weather and climate intelligence with the BBC's journalism and reach, the broadcaster said.

Director general Matt Brittin said the partnership would mean "serving our audiences with the most accurate, reliable and helpful weather service we can".

But the launch comes during a savings drive at the corporation, which has seen some other weather services and bulletins dropped as part of wider cuts.

The new Met Office partnership is unrelated to the cuts and was announced last July, before the BBC embarked on its latest round of savings.

A new hourly forecast on the BBC News website and app covering 10 days, with improved medium-range forecasts

Met Office severe weather warning notifications via the BBC Weather app

More local and more digital weather reports, and more forecasts fronted by local weather presenters

More "content collaboration on BBC and Met Office channels" using Met Office expertise, and helping to explain weather and climate

There will also be Met Office branding on weather reports, and a new BBC weather centre based in the agency's headquarters in Exeter.

Brittin said the collaboration would involve "turning science into stories and helping audiences make informed decisions with our forecasts".

Met Office chief executive Penny Endersby said: "Today is a landmark moment as the Met Office and the BBC join forces to give even more people across the UK access to Met Office's accurate and trusted weather information."

She added: "Our new partnership with the BBC combines the Met Office's world-leading science with the BBC's incredible reach, giving a powerful opportunity to bring the story of our changing weather and climate to millions more people."

A previous partnership between the BBC and the Met Office ended in 2018.

Since 2018, the BBC's data for its weather forecasts has been provided by the Dutch MeteoGroup, which was later acquired by US weather services company DTN.

Separately, the BBC has dropped or shortened a number of national television and radio weather bulletins in recent weeks, as the corporation continues to work towards a £500m savings target.

Some weekend and late-night forecasts have been dropped from the TV schedules, with regional presenters instead now delivering a UK-wide weather outlook during their presenting slots.

Listeners have also complained about programmes such as Radio 4's PM no longer delivering a full weather bulletin, with presenter Evan Davis instead reading a short summary and directing listeners to the BBC website for a more detailed forecast.

The BBC said it was changing its weather team to better serve digital platforms, in line with audience research and changing consumption habits.

The corporation said more users are accessing weather information via the BBC's app, website and social platforms, as the number of people relying on broadcast bulletins declines.

A spokesman for the corporation said: "The BBC is committed to providing a world-class public service for weather forecasting and information across our platforms.

"As we announced in July, we are making changes to the way we deliver weather information as more people are turning to mobile and the website for their weather forecasts. We also recognise that people want more local forecasts, along with the national picture, to help them plan their coming days more accurately.

"As such we are providing more digital and localised forecasts, as well as ensuring we still have appropriate national weather bulletins across the TV and radio."

BBC Radio 4's Today programme, BBC Breakfast and the weekday editions of BBC One's News at Six will retain their usual national weather forecasts.

articles.title: Zambia bans protest against push to remove presidential term limits
articles.summary: Critics fear the campaign could undermine democratic safeguards as senior opposition figures remain behind bars.
articles.body:
Lusaka, Zambia – Zambian authorities have banned a planned protest against calls to remove presidential term limits, amid mounting concerns over political freedoms following President Hakainde Hichilema’s disputed re-election in August.

The demonstration, scheduled for November 25, was organised by civil society groups and human rights defenders opposed to proposals that could allow Hichilema to remain in power beyond 2031, when his second and final five-year term is due to end.

Police cited the risk of clashes after a pro-government youth group announced plans to hold a rival demonstration in support of removing presidential term limits.

Three organisations aligned with the governing United Party for National Development (UPND) have petitioned the National Assembly to remove constitutional restrictions on presidential terms, potentially paving the way for Hichilema to seek a third term.

The campaign has drawn opposition from civil society organisations, the influential Catholic Church and the Law Association of Zambia (LAZ), which have called for an end to the debate over extending presidential tenure.

Hichilema, who swept to power in 2021 on a promise of democratic reforms, had repeatedly criticised African leaders who sought to extend their rule through constitutional amendments.

His office has sought to reassure critics. In a statement on November 20, presidential communications official Clayson Hamasaka said Hichilema would respect the constitution “at all times”.

“The president also respects every citizen’s right to freedom of expression,” Hamasaka said.

But the campaign to remove term limits, coupled with the prolonged detention of senior opposition figures, has raised concerns among government critics about the future of one of Africa’s more established multiparty democracies.

On November 4, civil society organisations and human rights defenders notified police of their intention to march against the removal of presidential term limits.

A pro-government youth alliance subsequently announced plans to demonstrate in support of the proposals, prompting police to cite the risk of confrontations between the two groups.

Minister of Home Affairs and Internal Security Clement Andeleki defended the decision to cancel the demonstrations, dismissing suggestions that Hichilema was seeking a third term.

“We cancelled [the protests] because those are trying to go to the streets, they are going to do what? Because there is no third term that the president [Hichilema] wants,” Andeleki told Al Jazeera.

The decision came days after Justice Minister Jack Mwiimbu pledged to protect citizens exercising their right to petition parliament for the removal of presidential term limits.

“We’ll not allow individuals threatening others who are exercising their rights to express themselves freely,” Mwiimbu told journalists in Lusaka on November 18, adding that Hichilema would respect any amendments to the constitution.

Linda Kasonde, a former president of the Law Association of Zambia and one of the organisers of the planned demonstration, said the group had appealed against the police decision.

“We have seen that we are being blocked from protesting and so, we have written to the police to give us an alternative date and we have also written to the minister of home affairs to appeal the decision of police,” Kasonde told Al Jazeera.

She said the organisers remained committed to peaceful protest and wanted to demonstrate public opposition to the removal of presidential term limits.

A disputed election and opposition crackdown

The controversy comes against the backdrop of a disputed general election and the detention of some of Hichilema’s most prominent political opponents.

Hichilema was re-elected in August with more than 61 percent of the vote in an election in which observers, including the European Union Election Observation Mission, reported irregularities.

A six-hour suspension of vote counting and the announcement of results, the deployment of soldiers at polling stations and tallying centres, and the removal of opposition and independent monitors raised questions about the credibility of the electoral process.

The closure of courts following the election also raised concerns over the opposition’s ability to challenge the results.

Brian Mundubile, who finished second in the presidential race and accused Hichilema of electoral fraud, was arrested alongside his running mate, Makebi Zulu, in a post-election crackdown.

Then, former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was fatally wounded by security forces during a raid on a house in Lusaka where senior opposition figures were meeting.

Mundubile, Zulu and several other opposition figures have been detained for more than 100 days over allegations of attempting to overthrow Hichilema’s government and engaging in seditious activities.

The accused say the charges are politically motivated.

Their prolonged detention has drawn condemnation from local and international human rights defenders and prompted a legal challenge against the state.

A day before the High Court was due to rule on their continued detention, prosecutors produced a charge sheet alleging treason.

Sakwiba Sikota, a leading defence lawyer, told Al Jazeera that the trial was expected to begin in 2027.

Treason is a non-bailable offence in Zambia and carries a possible life sentence. Lengthy legal proceedings could keep some of the country’s most prominent opposition figures out of public life for monthsm or even years.

Muhabi Lungu, secretary-general of the Tonse Alliance, the opposition coalition led by Mundubile, alleged that the prosecutions were intended to weaken the opposition ahead of possible constitutional changes.

“This scheme was hatched a long time ago, and so, this treason issue is an attempt to try and denigrate the opposition so that somehow, they can justify why he must continue beyond the constitutional requirement,” Lungu told Al Jazeera.

He urged the authorities to expedite the trial and make public the evidence against the accused.

The battle over presidential term limits

Supporters of the proposed changes argue that presidential term limits restrict voters’ democratic right to choose their leaders.

Mark Simuuwe, the UPND’s head of media, rejected suggestions that the campaign was specifically intended to secure a third term for Hichilema.

“We are not talking about a third term bid here; instead we are talking about removal of the term limit restrictions because we feel the current constitution is undemocratic as it denies electorates a chance to elect a president of their choice when they want to,” Simuuwe said in an interview.

A constitutional amendment would require the support of at least two-thirds of parliamentarians, although additional constitutional procedures may apply to changes affecting presidential tenure.

The UPND does not command a two-thirds majority in the National Assembly but could seek support from independent legislators and other members of parliament.

For critics, however, removing presidential term limits would risk dismantling an important democratic safeguard in a country that has experienced several peaceful transfers of power since the introduction of multiparty democracy in 1991.

Among them was Hichilema’s own election victory in 2021, when he defeated incumbent President Edgar Lungu.

The debate in Zambia comes as constitutional changes elsewhere in Africa have renewed concerns over presidential tenure and democratic accountability.

In neighbouring Zimbabwe, President Emmerson Mnangagwa signed into law constitutional amendments in July that would allow him to remain in office two years beyond his previous term limit.

The amendments extend presidential terms from five to seven years and replace direct presidential elections with a system under which parliament selects the president.

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, another of Zambia’s neighbours, President Felix Tshisekedi has approved legislation allowing constitutional changes to be put to a referendum, a development that critics fear could pave the way for a third presidential term.

In Zambia, the debate over term limits is unfolding as opposition leaders remain behind bars and civil society groups await a response from the authorities on whether they will be allowed to demonstrate.

For Kasonde, the campaign to remove term limits cannot be separated from the political tensions that followed the August election.

“This attempt to remove the term limits to consolidate power is not for ideological reasons but because of the [decline in] legitimacy following a controversial election,” she said.

articles.title: The US pastor who wants to see women's right to vote overturned
articles.summary: The movement to repeal women's right to vote has gained traction amongst some very conservative Christians.
articles.body:
"Patriarchy is in accordance with the way God made the world." That is the view of Pastor Doug Wilson, a conservative minister who the US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth calls his mentor.

Speaking to the BBC from his base in Moscow, Idaho, Wilson explained his view that a society led by men is "a very great blessing". It's a perspective Christians who disagree with him say is based on a fundamentalist understanding of the Bible, which promotes the subjugation of women.

A self-described Christian nationalist, Wilson believes the US should be a theocracy, with gay sex criminalised, abortion outlawed, and people of other faiths unable to hold public office.

In the past he has delivered a sermon on "The Lost Virtue of Sexism," arguing that the Bible says women should be excluded from leadership of the church, and certain roles in civic affairs. And as part of his views on the division between the sexes, he would like the 19th Amendment of the US constitution, which granted women the right to vote, to be repealed, something his detractors say is anti-democratic.

The vast majority of Christians support women's right to vote, and dismiss his message as misogynistic and extreme.

Rev. Canon Dana Colley Corsello, the vicar at the Washington National Cathedral, rejects Wilson's understanding of what the Bible says about women's roles.

"In my mind, there is no biblical precedent or standing for what [Wilson has] proposed," she told the BBC.

"I'm married, I have a husband, I have children. My husband and I are complete equals in everything we do."

But while Wilson still represents a fringe perspective amongst Christians in the US, some of his views have been gaining support.

The denomination he co-founded, the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches (CREC), has around 150 churches in the US. It's a drop in the ocean compared to the 350,000 or so other Christian congregations the US. But Wilson says membership continues to rise.

His influence has grown in part because of his connection to Pete Hegseth. The Secretary of Defence is a "proud member" of a CREC affiliated church, a Pentagon spokesperson told the BBC, adding that the "secretary very much appreciates many of Mr. Wilson's writings and teachings".

Wilson says the two have "a warm relationship", although he stresses it is "largely a pastoral one, not a political one". Wilson has led prayer services at the Pentagon, including one in mid-November.

Joining Wilson on stage, Pete Hegseth said "thank you for your leadership, for your mentorship, for the things you've started, the truth you've told, your willingness to be bold."

Hegseth worships at the Washington, DC branch of Wilson's network of churches. And there are other members of the current administration that worship there too, according to Wilson.

Of all his views, it is his statements on women's suffrage that have garnered the most headlines.

Wilson favours "household voting", where the head of the home – usually a man – votes on behalf of their family. It's the system used for elections within his church, although the women in Wilson's family do vote in civic elections in order to counter votes of liberals, he says.

He says only in "odd" circumstances, such as divorce or bereavement or "where the husband was a quadriplegic," should women assume the role of head of household. Just 7% of votes in Wilson's church polity are cast by women.

When challenged by the BBC, he admitted it was a system that gave men "outsized influence".

Wilson says that repealing the 19th Amendment is "low" on the list of priorities for him and his congregation. But, he adds, "we do think it".

Julie Ingersoll, a professor of religious studies at the University of North Florida, says Wilson's beliefs are misogynistic and extreme - part of a world view that says women should be in complete submission to men in every part of their lives.

It is extremely unlikely that the 19th Amendment would be repealed - it would require either a proposal from two-thirds of the House and Senate or two-thirds of the state legislatures. Three quarters of states would then need to ratify it.

Still, says Ingersoll, the threat to women's rights should be taken seriously.

"It's not unlike the battle that they waged against Roe versus Wade," she says, referencing the Supreme Court decision that granted women the right to an abortion. It was overturned in 2022, after years of legal battles that restricted women's access to abortion.

"Thirty years ago, people would have said, oh, they're not gonna undo abortion rights.

"But they chipped away and they kept chipping away until they were able to overturn it. And I see this as directly parallel."

While Wilson says overturning the 19th Amendment could take a century or more, there are conservative Christians who are pushing for women to have their right to vote removed more immediately.

Last February, pastor Dale Partridge posted on Instagram saying "We will repeal the 19th Amendment within ten years".

Partridge, who has around 900k followers across social media, credits Wilson as being someone who "broke the ice" for "strong politics and theology".

Partridge has said that "the majority of women are not capable of responsible voting" because too many of them are liberal.

He also frequently collaborates on podcasts with another conservative pastor named Joel Webbon.

Webbon, whose New Christian Right YouTube channel has more than 190k subscribers, has said that women's "desires are wicked". The solution, he claims, is to "take away women's vote". He was once friendly with Wilson, although they have since fallen out.

"Those guys have overshot by a long way," says Wilson of the two younger pastors. "They are disruptors and basically rage baiting."

So what might be driving those who support the effort?

Kelly Marino, an associate professor at Sacred Heart University who studies women's suffrage, says that the last decade has seen big wins for the women's rights movement, and "liberal political ideology" in general.

But, she argues, "any time where there was sort of this peak of feminism, there've been people who respond aggressively and try to push back".

Added to that are the high levels of uncertainty and conflict that have characterised the post-Covid period.

"I think there's been this craving for tradition and things that felt safe," Marino says.

That, she says, can be seen in the popularity of notions such as being a "tradwife" or "soft girl", who reject career goals in favour of traditionally female roles of wife and mother.

Marino says that while she doesn't think the constitution could be changed in the immediate future, the conversation around repealing the 19th Amendment is shaping the way people think about women's roles in general.

Canon Corsello, the Vicar at Washington Cathedral, sees the midterm election results as a repudiation of the push against women's rights.

"Cultural issues did not translate in this election", she says. "When people are preaching love, empathy, inclusion... that actually resonated with people".

Wilson's views have, however, been gaining ground beyond the US. The CREC has more than 30 churches internationally, including in Poland, Japan and Brazil.

The latter country has seen its own movement of right-wing influencers pressing for the removal of women's suffrage, with some leaning on religious language to make their point.

Wilson wants to continue expanding his brand of Christianity around the world, and has recently accepted a church in England into his network.

While CREC churches in each country have their own distinct characteristics, Wilson says their core beliefs are the same.

When it comes to the US, he says his ideal scenario would be for his congregations to "to practice what we believe in the church and for outsiders to look at that and envy it and say, man, that seems like a good system".

A brown butter apple streusel pie available at Jamagansett, a bakery in the Hamptons in New York, costs $80, as does a cranberry pecan pie. articles.title: Storms push Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City to Saturday
articles.summary: The parade, which marks its 100th edition, got a last-minute rain check ahead of heavy gusts on Thursday.
articles.body:
New York City is famous for its annual Thanksgiving Day Parade, a procession of towering helium balloons, elaborate floats and marching bands.

But on Wednesday, organisers in the United States announced that this year’s edition has been postponed because of an East Coast storm that threatens turbulent weather.

It was rescheduled for Saturday instead, right after Black Friday, a day when retailers traditionally offer holiday shopping and discount prices.

The annual parade is sponsored by Macy’s, a New York-based department store brand, and Saturday’s event will be its 100th Thanksgiving procession.

“While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our participants and spectators is and always will be our top priority,” Will Coss, Macy’s executive producer, said in a Wednesday news conference.

“ We’re saddened by the shift, but we’re optimistic about our opportunity to deliver the most spectacular 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, the best and biggest parade in our history.”

The parade, founded in 1924, was cancelled three times during World War II, but this year marks the first time it was postponed.

The event’s signature balloons were already being inflated on Wednesday when Macy’s announced the delay.

The decision came amid warnings issued by the National Weather Service of lashing winds and possible coastal flooding for the New York City area.

Gusts are forecast to reach up to 97 km/h, and rainfall of 2.5 to 5cm is expected from Thursday into Friday. A high wind warning is also in effect from 10am local time (15:00 GMT) Thursday through 1am (6:00 GMT) Friday.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani described the decision as tough but necessary given the forecast.

“I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences. Yet safety has to come first,” he said at Wednesday’s news conference. “On Saturday, when balloons climb into the sky, every New Yorker and everyone visiting will be able to take in a show that is both truly spectacular and also safe.”

The holiday extravaganza typically draws more than 3.5 million spectators along its Manhattan route, according to New York City authorities. It is also broadcast nationwide.

For many Americans, the parade is a fixture of Thanksgiving, and the postponement marks a break with a familiar holiday ritual.

NBC, the television network that airs the annual parade, said it would instead broadcast a repeat of the 2025 edition on Thursday.

It remains unclear whether the full roster of performers scheduled for the parade will continue to perform on Saturday. According to Macy’s website, singers like Raye and Wyclef Jean were scheduled to headline, as were actors and Broadway stars like Leslie Odom Jr and Anthony Ramos.

New floats include a five-storey-tall balloon of the cartoon character Bluey wearing a crown, and a 17-meter-long version of the beagle Snoopy carrying his bird sidekick Woodstock.

There will also be a blue hippopotamus, a nod to the balloon that floated off from the 1931 parade and was lost.

Mamdani assured New Yorkers that the parade route would be safe once the storm passes on Saturday, thanks to a surge of law enforcement.

“ There will be an expanded police presence this Saturday along the route, and the [New York Police Department] is fully prepared for an event of this magnitude, just as they have been prepared for the 99 parades that preceded this,” Mamdani said.

“I want to make clear that there are no known specific or credible threats to the parade at this time.”

The festivities are slated to begin at 8:30am local time (13:30 GMT).

articles.title: California warns of flooding as King Tides peak over Thanksgiving
articles.summary: Parts of the Canadian province of British Columbia may also be affected by the storms and flooding, which come as millions of people travel for the holiday.
articles.body:
Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday.

Water levels across the US state's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service (NWS) - breaking records set just last month.

The NWS has warned parts of California could face major coastal flooding, which is likely to be significant in low-lying areas. There have already been some reports of flooding.

Meanwhile, storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia, and eastern parts of the US.

Portions of a pier in northern California came crashing down into the ocean on Wednesday as high tides and strong waves battered the structure, video showed.

Beachgoers have been advised to stay away from the water's edge as large waves could suddenly form. Such waves could be damaging to piers and jetties, and could capsize small vessels, the NWS warned.

Flooding has already been reported in the San Francisco Bay Area.

In San Diego, a high tide of 8 ft 11in was recorded on Wednesday morning local time - potentially breaking the record for highest tide measured in the area, which was just set late last month at 7.98ft.

In Los Angeles, the tide on Wednesday was thought to be as high 8.19 - the record for the city that was set only weeks ago 27 October when parts of the California coast experienced flooding.

Recently set high tide records were also broken in Santa Barbara and La Jolla, according to preliminary data.

King tides are the highest predicted tide of the year and are above the highest water level reached at high tide on an average day.

While they typically occur once or twice a year in most coastal areas, they are happening more frequently in some as sea levels rise. These king tides are being strengthened by the strongest El Niño weather pattern on record.

Storm systems are also expected to impact the US through the Thanksgiving holiday - one affecting the Pacific Northwest and another the eastern part of the country, the US National Weather Service said.

On the east coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding.

Major impacts are expected to begin on Wednesday across the southeast, and move northward Wednesday night and on Thursday, the NWS said.

"Those along the eastern seaboard can expect gusty, possibly damaging winds, heavy rain, and major coastal and marine impacts," it added.

The developing storm system could bring about one to four inches rain along America's east coast and a peak of four to six inches in coastal North Carolina.

The US department store chain Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, which was due to take place on Thursday, until Saturday because of severe weather - the first time this has happened.

The stormy weather on both coasts could disrupt travel for millions of people.

The American Automobile Association (AAA) has predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.

Officials have also issued a flood warning along Vancouver's coastline in Canada's most western province of British Columbia.

Residents were urged to take "immediate action to protect life and property", a weather warning from Environment and Climate Change Canada said.

King tides were expected to potentially increase already high water levels there too.

articles.title: Ukraine attacks Russian military base, says five planes struck
articles.summary: The Ukrainian General Staff says its forces struck an airbase in the Nizhny Novgorod region east of Moscow.
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces have hit a major Russian military base east of Moscow, damaging five aircraft used to launch missiles and bombs, according to the Ukrainian General Staff.

Ukraine struck the Savasleyka airbase in the Nizhny Novgorod region, the General Staff said on Wednesday, adding that three MiG-31 jets were used to fire hypersonic missiles and two Su-34 fighter-bombers were damaged.

Russia did not immediately comment on the report by the General Staff, which said the Savasleyka airbase had been hit in the latest long-range attacks aimed at crippling Moscow’s war effort .

The operation followed a series of high-profile strikes by Ukrainian forces in recent days in which two Russian ships were hit in Libyan waters and a Russian vessel was struck in the Gulf of Finland .

Last week, Ukraine destroyed the road portion of Russia’s prized bridge to the Crimea peninsula after consecutive attacks.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and fighting has continued despite a renewed US-backed push to end what has become Europe’s worst conflict since World War II.

Kyiv is trying to dent Moscow’s military might as it struggles under a renewed campaign of attacks on its energy system and mounting Russian strikes on front-line cities.

Ukrainian forces are hunting Russian ballistic-missile launchers used to carry out many of those attacks, striking 16 over the past several months, Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said this week.

Renewed Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russian oil refineries’ processing volumes by 45 percent since late October, industry sources said this month. Kyiv has said it will stop striking Russian energy targets only when Moscow does the same.

articles.title: As foreign troops withdraw from Somalia, could al-Shabab take over?
articles.summary: Somalia relies heavily on foreign funding and military support for its very survival.
articles.body:
Somalia is facing a fresh test of its stability as foreign troops begin withdrawing, funding for its security forces comes under pressure and a bitter political dispute threatens to derail plans for the country's first direct democratic elections in decades.

The combination of challenges has raised questions about whether the government can defend itself against Islamist militant group al-Shabab while managing growing divisions among political factions.

Some analysts fear the situation could embolden al-Shabab, which is affiliated with al-Qaeda, and potentially allow it to seize control of the capital, Mogadishu.

The group already controls large parts of the country despite the presence of about 12,000 African Union (AU) troops supporting the government.

The withdrawal of foreign forces, alongside the activities of clan-based militias aligned with rival political factions, has heightened concerns about the government's ability to maintain control.

Ugandan troops, who make up the largest contingent of the AU force, began withdrawing last month, with the country expected to complete its withdrawal by next year.

Ethiopia, another major contributor to the AU mission, is also reportedly planning to withdraw about 3,000 troops. The country has 2,500 troops authorised under the AU mission and roughly 5,000 under a bilateral agreement with Somalia. It is not clear whether the reported withdrawals would be from the AU contingent, the bilateral force, or both.

The US, which had earlier announced cuts to funding for the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has since said it is extending it for a year. Washington contributes about a quarter of $500m UNSOS's annual budget, which supports Somali security forces, AU missions and individual troop-contributing nations.

With military support uncertain and the government facing mounting political challenges, analysts question whether Somalia's security forces are ready to stand on their own.

The concerns were heightened recently when al-Shabab claimed to have killed hundreds of elite Somali soldiers in an attack. The government acknowledged the attack but did not disclose the number of casualties.

Abdisalam Guleid, a former deputy director of Somalia's National Security Agency, told the BBC the security situation was increasingly precarious.

He warned that the withdrawal of foreign troops could leave Mogadishu vulnerable to a takeover similar to that of Afghanistan by the Taliban in 2021, following the withdrawal of US and Nato forces.

"I don't think Mogadishu will be able to defend itself. The Taliban style [takeover]… that's the most likely scenario I can envision now," he said.

The Taliban took over control of Afghanistan between 6-15 August 2021 in a rapid offensive, following the withdrawal of US and NATO forces.

Such a scenario has played out in Somalia in the past, Guleid explains.

Why is Uganda fighting in 'hellish' Somalia?

Somalia has experienced the collapse of central authority before.

In the early 1990s, clan-based rebel groups advanced on Mogadishu from several fronts, forcing then-President Mohamed Siad Barre from power.

His overthrow triggered a devastating civil war and a prolonged humanitarian crisis. The collapse of state institutions subsequently created conditions in which Islamist militant groups, including al-Shabab, were able to expand their influence.

Guleid says Ugandan troops have been central to preventing a similar collapse since their first deployment to Somalia in 2007.

They played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns, while protecting strategic installations, including the airport, seaport, government institutions and diplomatic missions.

Troops from Burundi, Djibouti, Kenya, Sierra Leone and Ethiopia later joined the AU mission, while countries including Turkey and the US maintained separate military deployments and provided training and equipment to Somali forces.

But Guleid argues that years of international assistance have not translated into sufficient military independence for the Somali government.

He says the authorities have become so reliant on foreign protection that they have neglected to adequately prepare their own forces to take over.

Somalia's Information Minister Abdifatah Qasim Mohamud rejected suggestions that the country would be unable to cope with the withdrawals.

He told the BBC that Somali troops had already taken over some positions vacated by Ugandan forces and were prepared to assume greater responsibility for the country's security.

He said Somalia could not depend indefinitely on foreign troops for its protection.

"I believe there is no reason for concern over this issue. There will be no change in the country's security situation or in the areas they have vacated," he said.

President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has also been seeking continued international backing.

During a visit to Uganda on 23 November, he and President Yoweri Museveni called on the international community to continue supporting Somalia to consolidate security gains.

Not everyone believes the withdrawal will necessarily result in a security collapse.

Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa argues that years of international military support have helped Somalia establish the institutions needed to take greater responsibility for its security.

He says the withdrawal will provide an opportunity to assess how much progress has been made.

It will also force Somalia's political leaders to put aside their differences and take greater responsibility for the country's future, he adds.

But other analysts warn that the timing could hardly be worse.

Omar Mahmood, an analyst at the International Crisis Group, says Somali forces are under considerable pressure as they fight al-Shabab while attempting to take over positions previously held by foreign troops.

This is a major undertaking for an army that is still developing, he says.

The military is also facing pressure in the Bay region of the South-West state, where forces loyal to ousted regional President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed have been fighting the federal government.

The withdrawal of Ugandan troops from the Lower Shabelle region could create further security challenges, Mahmood adds.

Mahmood further points to the long-delayed elections, which need to be secured, as another issue compounding the security situation.

Somalia has been attempting to move away from an indirect electoral system in which clan elders select lawmakers, who then elect the president, towards a system of direct voting.

Beyond the military situation, Mahmood says, the government must also resolve a growing political dispute over the timing and format of the country's elections.

But the proposed changes have divided the government and opposition, with disagreements over how the elections should be conducted.

The dispute escalated this year after Mohamud pushed through constitutional amendments extending the presidential term from four to five years, effectively delaying the next elections until 2027.

This month, the Supreme Court ruled against the extension, ordering political leaders to agree on an electoral roadmap within 30 days and to hold elections within three months.

A day before the ruling, Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed. He and other judges in the case have filed a suit against Somalia over the dismissals at the East African regional court in Tanzania.

The Somali government has since rejected the Supreme Court's decision, with its implementation now uncertain.

Mahmood says the political and security crises are closely connected, with the absence of consensus over the elections making it harder for the government to focus on the fight against al-Shabab.

Guleid also warns that the threat to Somalia's stability comes not only from the militant group but from clan-based militias increasingly challenging the federal government.

"Today, we have clan loyalists fighting alongside al-Shabab against the federal government," he said.

He added the country's leadership appears unable to anticipate the scale of the challenges ahead.

Who will fill the gap left by foreign partners?

Somalia's security challenges are compounded by its heavy dependence on international financial support.

Latest data from its finance ministry shows that donor grants amounting to $878.8m accounts for two-thirds of its planned $1.36bn budget in 2026.

Despite that, the ministry said it had only received about $314m of grants in the first nine months of the year, equivalent to 35% the expected annual aid.

Mahmood believes that although some international military support is declining, other partners could help bridge the gap through bilateral agreements and continued assistance.

But Guleid is sceptical that countries such as Turkey, Qatar and Egypt could quickly replace the military and financial contributions of Uganda and the US.

He argues that Somalia's dependence on external support makes it particularly vulnerable when international partners change their priorities.

That dependence has also contributed to increasingly strained relations with some foreign governments.

Somalia has accused the United Arab Emirates of funding armed groups and undermining its sovereignty, in the latest dispute involving an external power with significant security and economic interests in the country.

The UAE has rejected the criticism and hit back at the Somali leader, describing him as an "outgoing president" in reference to the dispute over his presidential mandate.

The two countries formally severed ties earlier this year, although the UAE has long been an important security and economic partner in Somalia.

The dispute illustrates the difficult relationship Somalia has with foreign partners on whom it relies for security, funding and political support.

For Egesa, the withdrawal of foreign troops could ultimately provide an opportunity for Somalia to demonstrate how much progress it has made in rebuilding its security institutions.

He believes the staggered departure of troops will allow Somali forces to assume responsibility gradually, while also forcing rival political factions to work together.

He argues that unless Somalia addresses its military weaknesses, political divisions and growing influence of armed groups, it risks losing the security gains made.

For now, it faces the difficult task of fighting an entrenched insurgency, managing rival political interests and preparing for a contentious electoral process, all while some of military partners are preparing to leave.

Whether Somalia can withstand these pressures without renewed instability remains an open question.

articles.title: UK government set to publish new treaties agreed with EU
articles.summary: The BBC understands the treaties contain a 10-year termination clause to reimburse costs of any need to rebuild border checks infrastructure.
articles.body:
The government and the EU are set to publish the texts of two treaties that were agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.

The treaties will be published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation which is designed to enact the bulk of the deal.

The BBC understands the treaties have a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.

Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch and Reform UK's Nigel Farage have suggested they would refuse to pay.

The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the long-term UK-EU relationship.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Two of the three legal texts will be released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.

New assessments of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country are also expected.

EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme

Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students

Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports.

The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."

The BBC understands that a plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.

The treaty text will also contain finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules.

Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, will also be detailed in the legislation.

Such powers could enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.

Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week , the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".

Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

Ahead of the Big Ten matchup between No. 15 USC and No. 9 UCLA, officials barred the Trojan Marching Band from its pregame and halftime shows after members allegedly vandalized signage at the Wasserman Football Center. articles.title: A Chandigarh woman on her way to receive 'Best Advocate Award' was left waiting for nearly two hours after her booked cab failed to arrive; consumer commission orders travel agency to pay Rs 10,000
articles.summary: CHANDIGARH: A cab that never arrived cost a Chandigarh woman nearly two hours on the morning she was supposed to travel to Ludhiana for an award ceremony.
articles.body: CHANDIGARH: A cab that never arrived cost a Chandigarh woman nearly two hours on the morning she was supposed to travel to Ludhiana for an award ceremony. With no response from the travel agency, she had to find another vehicle to make the journey. The incident dates back to August 28, 2022. Nearly four years later, a Punjab consumer commission has held the travel agency responsible for failing to provide the promised service and ordered it to pay Rs 10,000 in compensation and litigation expenses.The dispute centred on a booking made three days before the scheduled journey. The woman had contacted the agency on August 25 to arrange a Chandigarh-Ludhiana round trip. She was due to attend a function in Ludhiana, where she was reportedly set to receive the Best Advocate Award. The fare became part of the dispute. While the agency initially quoted Rs 2,200, the woman negotiated it down to Rs 2,000, an arrangement reflected in their WhatsApp conversation. She claimed that she had also paid Rs 1,000 in advance and was assured that the cab would pick her up from her residence at 6.30 am.That assurance was not honoured. When the vehicle failed to arrive, the woman tried reaching the agency but allegedly received no information about the delay. After waiting for around two hours, she made alternative transport arrangements and continued to Ludhiana. She subsequently approached the consumer commission, alleging harassment and embarrassment caused by the agency's failure. The agency disputed her version, arguing that the booking was never confirmed because she had not deposited 50% of the agreed fare as advance. It maintained that its representative had shared the number of an independent cab driver on August 27 and instructed her to contact him directly. It also denied receiving the Rs 1,000 payment or assuring her of a confirmed pickup.The commission's examination of the WhatsApp messages established that the two parties had discussed and agreed on the booking and fare. While the woman could not produce evidence of the alleged advance payment, the commission found that the agency could not deny that a cab had been booked but was not provided on time. The woman had also sought relief on the ground that she missed an important award ceremony. However, the commission noted that she had submitted no documentary evidence to establish that she was actually scheduled to receive the award or had missed the function.It nevertheless held that the absence of proof regarding the award did not excuse the agency's failure to provide the vehicle at the promised time. articles.title: A Punjab mason's son dreamed of moving abroad until his visa was rejected; instead, Ravinder Singh began raising free-range chickens and now sells eggs from a flock of around 700 hens from a street cart
articles.summary: For many young people in Punjab, moving abroad is seen as a way to escape financial struggles and build a better future.
articles.body: For many young people in Punjab, moving abroad is seen as a way to escape financial struggles and build a better future. Ravinder Singh, the son of a mason from Rataul village, once shared that dream. He imagined earning a good living overseas, but his plans came to an unexpected halt when his visa application was rejected.The disappointment left him uncertain about his future. However, instead of continuing to chase an opportunity abroad, Ravinder began looking for ways to earn a living closer to home. What followed was an unexpected journey into poultry farming.Today, he owns around 700 free-range hens and has built a small business selling their eggs directly to customers. His shop is not a conventional shopfront. Every day, he takes his produce to New Amritsar on a street cart, where customers have gradually started recognising his eggs. His journey, reported by The Tribune and Janta Se Rishta, is a reminder that sometimes a change in direction can open doors that were never part of the original plan.When a rejected visa changed the direction of his lifeGrowing up in a family with limited financial resources, Ravinder believed that working abroad could offer him a more secure future. Like several other youngsters from Punjab, he saw foreign employment as an opportunity to improve his family's circumstances. But when his visa was refused, the setback affected him deeply. He admitted that he felt low and struggled to figure out what to do next.Rather than allowing the disappointment to keep him from moving forward, he decided to explore opportunities within India. Poultry farming gradually caught his attention, and he began building a livelihood around raising chickens. Looking back, Ravinder believes the rejection ultimately pushed him towards something he enjoys and has managed to turn into a sustainable source of income. Speaking to The Tribune, he said, "At one time, I thought going abroad was the only way to earn a good living. When my visa was refused, I felt very low. But I decided to work hard here instead."From a flock of hens to a street-cart businessRavinder's business now revolves around approximately 700 hens raised through a free-range system. Unlike conventional poultry farming, where birds are generally kept in enclosed housing, free-range rearing allows chickens to move around in an open environment. This is the approach Ravinder has adopted for his flock.Instead of depending entirely on intermediaries or selling his produce through established shops, he has chosen to connect directly with customers. Every day, he loads the eggs onto his street cart, locally known as a rehri, and heads to New Amritsar. Selling directly allows him to build relationships with buyers and market his produce himself.The business has also benefited from seasonal demand. According to the report, sales are particularly encouraging during winter, when demand for eggs increases. Ravinder believes that more customers are becoming interested in eggs produced through free-range methods and are willing to purchase them directly from the farmer.A business that looks beyond selling eggsRavinder has also thought about how to make the most of his poultry business over the long term. His plan does not end when the hens become less productive at laying eggs. Once they reach that stage, he intends to sell them for meat, giving the birds another commercial purpose. This approach allows him to consider more than one source of income from his poultry operation. He also says that his financial position has improved considerably. In fact, he believes he is now doing better financially than some of his friends who moved to Italy in search of employment. His experience has changed his understanding of what it takes to build a successful livelihood. For him, going abroad is no longer the only route to financial stability.His message to young people: Start small, but keep movingHaving experienced disappointment and eventually found his footing through a small enterprise, Ravinder has a simple message for other young people who are uncertain about their futures. He believes that opportunities exist in India too, particularly in businesses connected to food and agriculture. He also encourages aspiring entrepreneurs to start with whatever resources they have rather than waiting for the perfect opportunity."Start small, but do not sit idle. Healthy foods have a growing market, and it also pays well. Instead of selling to the middlemen, market your produce yourself," he told The Tribune. For Ravinder, the journey from a rejected visa application to managing 700 hens has been about more than finding another way to earn money. It has been about discovering that a promising future does not always require crossing borders. The dream of moving abroad may have remained unfulfilled, but the opportunity he built at home has given him a different reason to look ahead.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 'Zero tolerance for terrorism': EAM Jaishankar remembers 26/11 victims on attack anniversary
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Thursday paid tribute to the victims of the 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks, remembering the innocent
articles.body: NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Thursday paid tribute to the victims of the 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks, remembering the innocent lives lost and the security personnel who made the supreme sacrifice while fighting the terrorists.Marking 18 years since the attacks that shook the country, Jaishankar reiterated India's commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and bringing those responsible to justice."Remember innocent lives lost & salute the brave security personnel who made the supreme sacrifice during 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks. Committed to combating terrorism in all its forms & manifestations and bringing those involved to justice. Zero tolerance for terrorism," Jaishankar wrote in a post on X.This year marks 18 years since 10 Pakistan-backed Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) terrorists launched a series of coordinated attacks across Mumbai, targeting some of the city's busiest locations.Commonly known as 26/11, the attacks began on the night of November 26, 2008, when the terrorists entered Mumbai by sea. Over the next four days, they carried out strikes at several locations, killing 166 people and injuring around 300.Among the targets were the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, the Oberoi-Trident Hotel, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, Nariman House, Cama Hospital, Metro Cinema and Leopold Cafe. Several of these locations were frequented by foreign nationals and Mumbai's workforce.The attacks left a lasting impact on the city, with the memories of the siege continuing to haunt survivors and families of those killed. Bullet marks at Leopold Cafe and Nariman House, along with memorials honouring the security personnel who lost their lives, remain reminders of the tragedy.Nine of the 10 terrorists were killed during the security operation, while the lone surviving attacker, Pakistani national Mohammad Ajmal Amir Kasab, was captured. Assistant Sub-Inspector Tukaram Omble played a crucial role in apprehending Kasab before succumbing to his injuries.Kasab was sentenced to death in May 2010 and hanged at Yerawada Central Prison in Pune on November 21, 2012.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
